exp.0:1:
This verse records the words of a decree issued by King Cyrus of Persia. He says that the God of heaven gave him authority over all the kingdoms of the earth and charged him to build a house, that is, the temple, at Jerusalem in Judah. "The LORD" is the name of God, and the word "build" in the verse means to construct.

Cyrus is the one speaking, but the text makes clear that God stirred his spirit to fulfill what had been announced through Jeremiah. The Jews had spent years in exile in Babylon. With this decree they were allowed to return and rebuild the temple. We cannot know for certain how far Cyrus believed in the LORD; some think he saw him as just one among the gods of the peoples.

For today: God can guide the events of history, even through people who do not know him well. If you are going through a situation that seems closed, trust that God keeps his promises in his own time, and stay ready to obey when he opens the door.
exp.5:6:
It says that the work of rebuilding God's temple in Jerusalem must not be hindered. The neighboring governors must let the governor of the Jews and their elders (the leaders of the people) build the house of God in its place, that is, on the same site where it stood before.

The one speaking is King Darius of Persia. Tatnai and his companions had questioned the work and written to the king. Darius ordered a search of the archives, found the earlier decree of King Cyrus that allowed the rebuilding, and now orders the opponents to stay away and even to help with the expenses.

For today: when a good work faces opposition, we can keep going with patience and confidence. God can open doors, even through unexpected people, and our task is to persevere in what He has entrusted to us.
exp.4:5:
This verse is like the heading of an official letter. It says that what follows is a copy (a "copy" of the message) of the letter that Tatnai, governor of the region west of the Euphrates River, and Shethar-boznai, together with their companions, the men from that region (probably other officials of the area), sent to King Darius.

The Jews who had returned from exile were rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem. Tatnai and his companions went to inspect the work and decided to consult the king. The previous passage says that God watched over the Jewish elders, and that is why they did not stop the construction while the answer was on its way.

For today: when someone questions or hinders what you do in faith and with a good conscience, do not despair. Keep going honestly and trust that God watches over his work, even when the decisions are in the hands of others.
exp.6:5:
It says that Ezra went up from Babylon toward Jerusalem. He was a diligent scribe, that is, an expert who was careful and devoted in the law of Moses, which God himself had given. Also, the king granted him everything he asked for, and the text explains why: the hand of the Lord was upon him. The phrase "the hand of the Lord" is a way of speaking of his help and favor.

The book does not say who wrote it, but Jewish tradition usually attributes it to Ezra. Here Ezra is presented as a priest descended from Aaron, before his journey with a group of Jewish exiles, in the time of the Persian king Artaxerxes. The author wants to show that the king's favor was no accident, but the work of God.

For today: Ezra prepared well and also trusted in God. We can study the Bible with steadiness and do our work with effort, while at the same time recognizing that if something turns out well, it is God who sustains us.
exp.9:11:
This verse says that all the people gathered answered with a loud voice and agreed with Ezra. The words "congregation" in the verse means the crowd or assembly. The phrase that appears in the older wording as "as you have said, so may it be done" simply means: "We will do what you have told us."

The people speaking here were the Israelites who had returned from exile. Ezra the priest had just confronted them because many had married women from other peoples, and this was pulling them away from God and from his covenant. They acknowledge their wrong and agree to correct it. How this was carried out afterward is a delicate matter that should be read carefully within the whole book.

For today: when God's Word shows us something crooked in our lives, it is not enough to feel sad or simply say "amen." God invites us to respond with humility and with concrete steps of obedience, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.4:0:
God sent two prophets, Haggai and Zechariah (son of Iddo), to speak to the Jews who lived in Judah and in Jerusalem. They spoke "in the name of the God of Israel," that is, with God's authority and not on their own initiative. The verse says the prophets "prophesied," meaning they delivered God's message.

The one telling the account is the writer of Ezra. The Jews had returned from exile, but the work on the temple had stopped because of opposition. The books of Haggai and Zechariah show that God used them to encourage the people to resume the building. After this message, Zerubbabel and Jeshua began to build again.

For today: when you feel discouraged and have set aside something God placed in your heart, listen to his Word and seek the encouragement of faithful brothers and sisters. God often uses simple voices to help us start again.
exp.9:24:
This verse begins the list of the laypeople, that is, Israelites who were neither priests nor Levites, who had married foreign women. Here six men from the family of Parosh are named: Ramiah, Jeziah, Malchiah, Miamin, Eleazar and Benaiah. Note that "Malchiah" appears twice; these were probably two different men with the same name. "Moreover" only indicates that the list continues.

Context: The book tells the story in the third person, and tradition attributes it to Ezra. After the return from exile, the people had mixed their faith with the customs of the neighboring peoples. Ezra led a public act of repentance, and the names of those involved were recorded. Interpreters debate how to understand this harsh measure, but the text shows a desire to become faithful to God again.

For today: God takes our faithfulness seriously, and his lists of names show that every person counts. Ask him today to show you one area where you need to return to him, and take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.3:12:
It says that if Jerusalem is rebuilt and its walls are set up firmly, the people will no longer pay the taxes owed to the king. "Tribute" is the general tax, "toll" is a compulsory payment to the government, and "custom" refers to other payments or dues. "Endamage" means diminished or harmed. The word "revenue" in this version is of uncertain translation; it most likely refers to the king's income or treasury.

The speakers are the regional officials who opposed the Jews who had returned from exile. They write to King Artaxerxes to halt the work. They play on the fear of losing money and power, and they present Jerusalem as a threat. It is a self-interested accusation, not a neutral report.

For today: before believing an accusation against someone, let us ask what interests the person making it has. And if we are unjustly accused while doing what is right, let us trust that God sustains his work.
exp.0:0:
This verse says that in the first year of Cyrus as king of Persia, God moved his heart so that what the prophet Jeremiah had announced would be fulfilled. The phrase "stirred up the spirit" means that God impelled him or encouraged him to act. Cyrus issued a proclamation, that is, a public announcement, and he also put it in writing for his whole kingdom.

The book of Ezra begins after the people of Judah had spent decades in exile in Babylon. The one speaking here is the narrator, who shows God at work even through a foreign king. Jeremiah had announced that the exile would have an end (Jeremiah 29:10). Cyrus's decree allowed the Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple.

For today: God can fulfill his promises in unexpected ways, using people and circumstances we would not imagine. When the waiting grows long, we can keep trusting that God does not forget his word.
exp.7:22:
This verse says that the people fasted, that is, they stopped eating for a while to seek God with humility, and they asked him for protection on the journey. The word "propitious" means favorable, kind. God heard their prayer and answered them well.

Ezra speaks here, a priest and teacher of the law who was leading a group of Jews from Babylon to Jerusalem. They were carrying children, possessions, and a valuable offering for the temple. The road was dangerous. Ezra had told the king that God cares for those who seek him, and he felt ashamed to ask for soldiers. He preferred to trust God and to pray together beside the river Ahava.

For today: before a journey, an important decision, or a moment of risk, we can pray with humility and trust God, without failing to act with wisdom.
exp.1:6:
This verse says that the descendants of Elam, a family or clan of Israel, who returned from exile were one thousand two hundred fifty and four people. "Children of" here means descendants or members of that family, not only direct sons.

The book of Ezra gives a list of the Jews who returned to Jerusalem and Judah after the exile in Babylon, under permission from King Cyrus. The author, traditionally identified with Ezra, records family by family. This served to confirm the identity of the people and their right to the land and to worship. The numbers in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 have small differences, and scholars explain them in various ways, without full agreement.

God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Every family was remembered and counted. Today you can rest in the knowledge that your name and your story matter to God, and you can also value the people in your church who are small or little noticed.
exp.7:33:
It says that everything they brought to Jerusalem was counted and weighed carefully, and that the total weight was written down at that time. The word "wrote down" here means it was recorded and put in writing. Nothing was handed over by guesswork or from memory.

The speaker is Ezra, the priest and scribe, who tells in the first person the return of the exiles from Babylon. King Artaxerxes and other people had given silver, gold, and vessels for the temple. On arriving, on the fourth day, Ezra handed them over to priests and Levites, weighing them in the presence of witnesses. In this way it was clear that nothing had been lost on the way and that everything was for God.

For today: if we handle money or goods belonging to the church, the family, or the workplace, it is wise to do so with order, clarity, and honest records. Transparency protects trust, guards our witness, and honors God.
exp.6:17:
It says that Ezra and his brothers, the Jews, could use the rest of the silver and the gold however seemed good to them, provided they did it according to the will of God.

Here King Artaxerxes speaks in an official letter that he hands to Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law. He sends him to Jerusalem with permission and resources for worship in the temple. First the letter mentions the use of the offerings for the sacrifices; then the king leaves the remainder free to be used, but places it under the will of the God of Israel. Some think the king was also seeking the favor of God over his kingdom, although the text does not say this in those words.

When God gives us resources, we have freedom to decide, but not freedom to forget Him. Before using your money or your time, ask Him: "Lord, how do you want me to use it?"
exp.6:11:
This verse is the greeting that opens King Artaxerxes' letter. He calls himself "king of kings," a title used by Persian kings, and addresses Ezra as the priest and scribe of the law of the God of heaven. The word "scribe" here points to someone thoroughly trained in the law and able to explain it fully.

The verse ends with a shortened greeting, so the sentence stops before the full blessing is spelled out.

The king of Persia is the one speaking, and he gives Ezra official permission to return to Jerusalem. The text just before this says that Ezra had prepared his heart to study, practice, and teach the law of God. The letter gives him authority and support, and it allows other Israelites to go with him.

For today: Ezra first studied, then practiced, and then taught. If you want to serve God with influence, begin by setting aside time to learn his Word and to live it out sincerely.
exp.1:42:
This verse begins the list of the Nethinims, who were servants of the temple. The names Ziha, Hasupha and Tabbaoth are heads of families whose descendants returned to Jerusalem. The word "Nethinims" roughly means "those given" or "those dedicated," that is, people set apart to serve the temple. Some think their origin lay in workers assigned to the Levites, but the Bible does not give all the details.

Ezra the scribe records here the Jews who returned from exile in Babylon. This list arranged the people by families and duties, to restore the life of the temple and confirm who belonged to God's people. After the singers and gatekeepers, these helpers follow.

God remembers and values those who serve in quiet ways and without applause. Their names were written down. Today, your humble service in the church, at home or with your neighbors also matters to God. Serve him faithfully, even when few notice.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that 623 descendants of the family of Bebai returned from exile. "Children of" means members of a family or clan, not only direct sons. It is part of a list of names and figures.

Ezra 2 records the Israelites who returned from Babylon to Judah and Jerusalem, after King Cyrus allowed their return. Tradition attributes the book to Ezra, although this passage is only a record. Nehemiah 7:16 gives a different figure for Bebai (628). It is explained in several ways, for example by different moments of the count or by copying, but this is not known with certainty.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Every family and every person counts for Him. Today you can value those who serve without being noticed, and remember that your name and your effort matter to God.
exp.1:66:
This verse counts the animals the people brought back from exile: four hundred and thirty-five camels and six thousand seven hundred and twenty donkeys. The donkeys were the beasts of burden, used for carrying loads and for traveling. Together with the horses and mules of the previous verse, this shows how much equipment they needed for the long road home.

The author, traditionally identified with Ezra, keeps a record of those who returned from Babylon to Judah under the permission of King Cyrus. He notes even the animals because he wanted to leave an orderly account that God had brought his people back. The figures in this chapter do not fully match those in Nehemiah 7, and scholars explain this in several ways, with no certain answer.

For today: God pays attention to what seems small. Even the donkeys were written down. What you place at God's service, though it may be simple or modest, does not go unnoticed by him.
exp.7:27:
Ezra tells twelve priests that they are set apart for the Lord, just like the vessels they are to carry. He also says that the silver and the gold were a freewill offering to God.

Ezra speaks before leaving Babylon for Jerusalem. He hands the priests the offerings for the temple and reminds them that these are not ordinary possessions. That is why they are weighed carefully, so that they can be delivered in full. The details of the journey are told in this same chapter.

Today we can remember that what God entrusts to us, whether money, gifts, or time, is a holy responsibility. A practical application is to manage it with honesty and order, and to give an account openly, as one who serves the Lord.
exp.9:41:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions three men: Shallum, Amariah, and Joseph. They were among the sons of Bani, according to the group named in the verses before. These are men who had taken foreign wives.

The book of Ezra records this list after the return from exile in Babylon. Ezra, the priest and scribe, led the people to acknowledge their sin: they had married women from neighboring peoples, which the law of Moses warned against because of the risk of turning them away from the God of Israel. The author notes the names one by one. How each family case was resolved is something the text does not detail, and there is discussion about how to understand this measure.

For today: God sees each person by name, and does not let the truth pass by. We can ask Him to show us where we need to return to Him, and respond with humility, hiding nothing.
exp.7:5:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned to Jerusalem with Ezra. It says that from the family of Adin came a leader named Ebed, son of Jonathan, and with him fifty men. The word "men" simply means men, and "sons of Adin" refers to the descendants of that family.

The one speaking is Ezra, the priest and scribe, who writes in the first person in this passage. He carefully records the heads of families who went up from Babylon, probably around 458 B.C., to rebuild the spiritual life of the people. Adin also appears in other lists in Ezra and Nehemiah, although the numbers vary.

For today: God pays attention to each person, not only to the great names. Ebed and his fifty men were recorded for having answered the call. Serve God faithfully where you are, even when no one applauds you; he does remember it.
exp.6:1:
This verse continues the list of Ezra's ancestors. It names three people: Shallum, Zadok and Ahitub, each one the son of the previous one in the family line. "Ahitub" is the spelling used in the verse above. Here "son of" may mean a direct son or a descendant, because in the Bible genealogies sometimes summarize several generations.

The author of the book, traditionally identified with Ezra, presents his family tree before telling about his journey to Jerusalem. This line connects him with Aaron and the priestly lineage. In this way the reader understands that Ezra had legitimate authority to teach the law and to guide the people. Some scholars note that the list leaves out names, and that this was not unusual in antiquity.

God works through generations. No one starts from zero: what your parents or teachers in the faith planted can prepare you to serve. Thank today those who passed on your faith, and think about what you can leave to those who come after you.
exp.1:15:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. It says that 98 people of the family of Ater returned, and they are identified as "of Hezekiah." This was probably meant to distinguish them from another family also called Ater (Ezra 2:42, where it appears in a different group). It is not known with certainty who that Hezekiah was.

The book of Ezra does not have a person speaking, but a record that tells how the people returned after King Cyrus decreed their freedom. The list shows that God kept his promise to restore his people. Each family was counted because their place in the community and in worship mattered, and the genealogies protected the identity of the people.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless crowd. Every name and every family counts. If today you feel small or little noticed in your church, remember that God knows you, and your simple service is part of his work.
exp.7:21:
Here Ezra tells how he was ashamed to ask the king of Persia for soldiers and horsemen to protect them from enemies during the journey to Jerusalem. He had already told the king that the hand of God is good toward all who seek him, but that his power and his anger fall on those who forsake him. The words for the soldiers and horsemen in the verse refer to a band of soldiers and horsemen, and the anger spoken of here is God's wrath against those who forsake him.

Ezra speaks in the first person. He is leading a group of exiled Jews who are returning to Jerusalem with families and valuable objects for the temple. The road was long and dangerous. Since he had declared his confidence in God before the king, he did not want to contradict with actions what he had said with words. So he proclaimed a fast beside the river Ahava to ask God for protection.

For today: when you face a risk, seek God in prayer before relying only on human resources. Using prudence is not wrong, but try to make your decisions show the confidence you say you have in him.
exp.3:22:
When the copy of King Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum, Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they went quickly to Jerusalem and forced the Jews to stop the work, using force and authority.

The narrator of the book is describing the outcome of an accusation. These officials had written to the king saying that rebuilding Jerusalem would bring rebellion. The king ordered the work stopped. They used the order to enforce it harshly. Some scholars debate how this fits with the temple work mentioned later.

For today: sometimes good work is slowed by unjust opposition. This does not mean God has abandoned you. Keep trusting, pray, and wait for his timing, because the story continues.
exp.1:29:
This verse says that 156 descendants of Magbish returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. "Children of" means relatives or descendants of the same family or place. Magbish appears only in this list in Ezra; it is not mentioned in Nehemiah 7, and we do not know for certain whether he was an ancestor or a town.

The author, traditionally Ezra, lists those who returned with Zerubbabel after the decree of King Cyrus. The list serves to show who belonged to God's people and to organize the life of the community, including worship and the land. That each group appears with its number shows that God kept his promise to bring his people back.

For today: God overlooks no one, not even those whom almost no one remembers. Your simple service and your name matter to him. You can be encouraged to take part faithfully in your community, without seeking recognition.
exp.6:14:
This verse is part of the instructions given to Ezra: to carry to Jerusalem the silver and gold that the king and his seven advisers had freely offered to the God of Israel. "Freely" means they gave it by their own choice, with no one forcing them to do so. "Habitation" is the place where God dwells, that is, the temple.

The speaker is the Persian king Artaxerxes, in an official letter. Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law, receives permission to travel with any Israelites who wished to go with him. The texts do not explain the king's motives in detail; they only show that he supported worship in the temple and the return of that group.

For today: giving generously and from the heart, without pressure, is one way of honoring God. We can ask ourselves what we freely offer: our time, our resources, or our service.
exp.7:31:
This verse says that Ezra and the group traveling with him finally arrived in Jerusalem and stayed there for three days. "Abode there" means they took time to rest and regain their strength. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem.

Ezra speaks, the priest and scribe, who tells the journey in the first person. He came from Babylon with returning exiles, carrying silver, gold and vessels for the temple. The road was long and dangerous, and he acknowledges that God watched over them. After the rest, on the fourth day, they handed over and weighed everything carefully in the temple.

For today: after a great effort, resting is not laziness, it is wise. We can thank God for His care, regain our strength, and then continue with responsibility and order in what He has entrusted to us.
exp.1:1:
The verse names eleven leaders who returned from exile with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. Then the count of the men of the people of Israel begins. The count here means the list of those men. Here there is a Nehemiah and a Mordecai, but it is not known whether they are the same people as in the books of Nehemiah and Esther. They are probably other people with the same name.

The book is anonymous, though tradition attributes it to Ezra. It records the return of the Jews to Judah after the exile in Babylon. The list shows that God kept his promise to bring his people back, and that every family mattered.

For today: God knows your name and values your place among his people. Even when you feel small or overlooked, your faithful service counts. Today you can help someone in your church without seeking recognition.
exp.1:17:
It says that the family of Jorah, that is, his descendants, numbered one hundred and twelve people among those who returned. The word "and" in the verse here reflects the old way of saying a number, and the phrase "children of" here means descendants or members of a clan.

This chapter is a list of the Jews who came back from Babylon to Judah, after King Cyrus allowed them to return. The author of the book, whom tradition identifies with Ezra, records each family carefully. In this way he shows that the people were real and that God was keeping his promise. In Nehemiah 7:24 a similar list appears with the name "Hariph"; perhaps it is the same family under another name, though this cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Even when your work seems small or no one notices it, he remembers it. Serve faithfully where you are.
exp.5:15:
The verse tells that the people celebrated with joy the dedication of the rebuilt temple in Jerusalem. Everyone took part: the children of Israel, the priests, the Levites (those responsible for service in the temple), and "the rest of the children of the captivity," that is, those who had returned from exile in Babylon.

The narrator of the book, whom tradition usually credits to Ezra, recounts the end of a work that had been halted by opposition and resumed with the encouragement of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah. After years of hardship, the temple was finished, and the people saw it as the work of God and of the Persian kings who had allowed it.

Today we can remember that when we finish something with God's help, it is worth stopping to thank him with joy and together as a community.
exp.0:2:
Here Cyrus invites the Jews who were living in exile to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple. The phrase "his God be with him" is a blessing: that God would accompany whoever decides to go. "Jerusalem" is the city of Jerusalem, and "the Lord" is the name of God. "All his people" refers to all the Israelites who were in the Persian kingdom.

Cyrus, king of Persia, speaks in the first year of his reign over Babylon, after Persia had conquered it. The text says that God stirred up his spirit to fulfill what had been announced through Jeremiah. Cyrus speaks in words that acknowledge the God of heaven, although historians debate what he actually believed.

God can move anyone, even a king who did not know him well, to fulfill his promises. If you feel a call to serve him, do not wait until you feel perfectly ready. Respond with faith, knowing that God walks with you.
exp.8:14:
Ezra says that God is righteous. If a small group of survivors still remains, it is because of God's mercy and not because of their own merit. Now they stand before Him with their guilt on their shoulders. Their sins are their own wrongdoing, and to remain standing means to hold up before God. He acknowledges that no one can come before God relying on their own innocence.

Ezra prays in Jerusalem, after the return from exile in Babylon. He learned that many of the people, including leaders, had married people from neighboring peoples and had adopted their idolatrous practices. Ezra does not defend himself or justify himself. He places himself in the people's position and confesses the sin as his own.

For today: when you fail, do not hide behind excuses or compare your fault with that of others. Come before God with sincerity, acknowledge your error, and remember that if you are still standing today, it is because of His mercy. That humility opens the door to forgiveness and change.
exp.9:34:
They are men from the family of Bani, mentioned along with others in the nearby verses. The text tells us nothing more about them.

The book of Ezra was written at the time when the Jews returned from exile in Babylon. Ezra, the priest and teacher of the law, tells here how some men of the people had married foreign women, and this drew them away from faithfulness to God. The list names those who acknowledged the wrong and committed themselves to correcting it. Interpreters debate how to apply this episode, since it was a painful decision and belongs to its particular context.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom almost no one remembers. He values the one who humbly recognizes their mistake and chooses to return to Him. Today we can ask Him for the courage to admit our failings and begin again.
exp.7:26:
This verse continues the list of the offerings that were weighed: twenty bowls of gold, worth a thousand drams, and two vessels of polished bronze, of very fine quality, as valuable as gold. "Clean metal" probably refers to bright bronze, although the text gives no further detail. A "dram" was a gold coin; the exact value of this figure is hard to determine.

Ezra, the priest and scribe, speaks about the return of the exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem. Before the journey, he carefully weighs the offerings from the king, his counselors, and the people, and hands them over to twelve priests so that they may guard them until they reach the temple.

For today: what is dedicated to God deserves honesty and order. We can care for church money and resources with transparency, and also for our time and talents, remembering that they belong to Him.
exp.7:0:
This verse presents a list of the heads of families who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. The chief men of each household or clan are the leaders of each family group. The record of their ancestors is the family line. All of this takes place during the reign of King Artaxerxes of Persia.

The speaker is Ezra, a priest and teacher of God's law. He writes in the first person ("went up with me"). He records the names to keep a record of who was part of this second group of returnees. The Jews carefully kept their family records because their identity as God's people and their service in the temple depended on them. Scholars debate the exact date, but the account shows God guiding his people back home.

God knows and values each person by name. Your simple and faithful work within your community also counts before Him, even when others do not notice it.
exp.5:7:
Here King Darius gives a clear order about how to treat the elders of the Jews who were rebuilding the temple. The money for the expenses was to come from the taxes the king collected in the region on the west side of the river Euphrates. It was to be given "forthwith," that is, without delay, "that they be not hindered," so that the work would not stop.

Darius is responding to a letter from Tatnai, a local governor, who doubted that the Jews had permission to build. The royal archives were searched and the earlier decree of Cyrus was found. That is why Darius not only confirms the permission but orders that the work be supported with resources from the kingdom.

For today: God can move even authorities who do not know Him to sustain what He has begun. We can pray with confidence over our work and, at the same time, labor with steadiness and honesty.
exp.6:8:
This verse tells how long Ezra's journey lasted. They left Babylon on the first day of the first month and arrived in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month. "It was the beginning of the journey" means that this is where the trip began. "Nethinim" were helpers of the temple. "The good hand of his God" means that God looked after him and showed him favor.

The narrator of the book describes how Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law, returned with a group of Israelites in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes. Many understand that the journey took about four months. The text makes clear right away that God helped them because Ezra had set his heart to study, practice, and teach the law of the Lord.

For today: God cares for those who walk with him, even on long and difficult journeys. Ask for his help in your plans, and prepare your heart with his Word, so that you may live it out and share it with others.
exp.6:12:
This verse is part of a decree from King Artaxerxes. He declares that any Israelite living in his kingdom, whether from the common people, a priest, or a Levite, may go with Ezra to Jerusalem if they wish to. The words "freewill" and "go" in the verse express that the choice is left to each person: whoever is minded of their own freewill may go.

The Persian king Artaxerxes speaks in an official letter addressed to Ezra. Many Jews were still living far from their land after the exile. The king gives Ezra authority and support to return to Jerusalem, teach God's law, and bring offerings for the temple. It is an open door, not an obligation.

For today: God knows how to open unexpected doors, even through authorities who do not know him. When he gives us an opportunity to serve him or to return to him, the response is voluntary, and it is good to give it with resolve and gratitude.
exp.1:8:
This verse is part of a list. It says that 760 descendants of the family of Zaccai returned to Judea after the exile. Zaccai was the name of an ancestor, and "children of" here means members of that family or clan, not only direct sons.

The book of Ezra presents this list of those who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem, after the decree of King Cyrus. The writer, according to tradition, is Ezra, a priest and scribe. The names and numbers are recorded to show that the people kept their identity. Some figures in this list appear differently in Nehemiah 7, and it is not known with certainty why; several explanations have been proposed.

For today: God pays attention to every family and every person, even to those whom almost no one remembers. Your name and your service, though they may seem small, matter to Him. Today, give thanks for someone who serves without being noticed.
exp.1:13:
This verse says that 2,056 people from the family of Bigvai returned. This is one of several entries in a list of families.

The book of Ezra does not have a narrator who identifies himself in this passage; Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra, though not everyone agrees. This list records those who returned from exile in Babylon to Judah, after the decree of Cyrus. Each family is noted to keep a record of who formed the restored people. Bigvai appears with a high number, among the larger groups.

For today: God pays attention to people, not only to great leaders. Each name and each number mattered. You can trust that God knows you, and that your part, even if it is simple, counts in what He is doing.
exp.1:65:
This verse is part of a list of the animals the Israelites brought with them on their return from exile. It says they had seven hundred thirty-six horses and two hundred forty-five mules. A mule is a beast of burden, the offspring of a horse and a female donkey. Together with the camels and donkeys in the following verse, these animals were their transport for the long journey.

Ezra, who writes as a chronicler and priest, carefully records how many returned to Judah from Babylon after the decree of King Cyrus. These lists show that God kept his promise to bring his people back. The numbers differ a little in other lists, such as the one in Nehemiah 7, and it is not known for certain why; several explanations have been proposed.

God pays attention to the small and the ordinary: every person and every animal counted in the rebuilding. You too have a place. Offer with joy what you have, whether much or little, to serve God and others.
exp.9:3:
This verse is a call to action. Shechaniah tells Ezra, "Arise," because the matter is his to lead. He promises support ("we also will be with thee") and encourages him to be brave ("be of good courage") and to carry it out ("do it"). "Matter" means business or responsibility. "Do it" means carry it out, put it into practice.

Shechaniah speaks on behalf of a group of the people who acknowledge that they disobeyed God by marrying women from neighboring peoples. Ezra was deeply distressed by this. Shechaniah proposes making a covenant and acting according to the law. His proposal is painful, and many readers find it difficult; the text presents it as an act of repentance for that moment.

When we recognize a wrong, sorrow alone is not enough; we must act. It also helps greatly to encourage and stand with the one who has the task of leading, instead of leaving him alone.
exp.1:32:
This verse says that 725 descendants, or inhabitants, of the towns of Lod, Hadid, and Ono returned from exile.

Since the verse reads "The children of Lod, Hadid, and Ono," the phrase "children of" here means descendants or people of that place.

The number 725 is the figure written out in the verse as "seven hundred twenty and five."

The author of the book, which tradition identifies with Ezra, copies here the list of those who returned to Judah from Babylon after the decree of King Cyrus. He notes families and towns one by one to record that they were part of God's people. Nehemiah 7:37 gives a slightly different figure (721). This is explained in several ways, but the reason for it is not known with certainty.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. He remembers each family and each place. Your service, even if it seems small or little seen, matters to God and is recorded before him.
exp.4:11:
This verse says that the ancestors of the Jews angered the God of heaven. For this reason He allowed Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, to destroy the temple and carry the people away into captivity in Babylon. The phrase "gave them into the hand of" means that God allowed that king to rule over them.

The speakers are the leaders of the Jews who had returned from exile. A Persian governor, Tatnai, asked them by what authority they were rebuilding the temple. They answer honestly: they acknowledge that the punishment was the consequence of their fathers' sin, and that they are now rebuilding because King Cyrus permitted it.

For today: being honest about our mistakes, without excuses, helps us to begin again. God corrects, but He also restores. If you recognize your failure and return to Him, you can rebuild what was broken.
exp.5:10:
Darius the Persian king orders a severe punishment for anyone who changes his decree about the temple. That person would have a beam pulled out of his own house, the beam would be raised up, and he would be hanged on it. Also, his house would be turned into a dunghill, an old-fashioned word meaning a heap of refuse or a place of waste. The word "alter" means to change, and the word "set up" means raised up.

The Persian king Darius speaks here. The governors of the region had questioned the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem. Darius confirmed the permission given earlier by Cyrus, and so protected the work and secured what was needed for the sacrifices. Some scholars debate the exact detail of the punishment, but its harshness was common in ancient decrees.

For today: God can guide the hearts of rulers and circumstances to accomplish his purposes. When you face opposition in something God has entrusted to you, pray, persevere faithfully, and trust that he cares for his work.
exp.5:4:
This verse says that the gold and silver objects of the temple, which Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon, were to be returned. They were to go back to their place, to the temple in Jerusalem, and be set down again in the house of God.

Here the decree of King Cyrus is cited, which was found in the archives of the kingdom. The governors of the region had questioned the Jews' permission to rebuild the temple, and King Darius ordered the document to be searched for. This confirmed that Cyrus had indeed authorized it and that he even provided the resources for the work.

For today: God knows how to care for what belongs to Him and keeps what He promises, even when many years pass. If you feel you have lost something precious in your faith or your life, trust that He can restore it. In the meantime, faithfully care for what He has entrusted to you.
exp.9:26:
This verse is part of a list of names. It names six men from the family of Zattu: Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad, and Aziza. The names are written in older spellings, but they are common Hebrew names.

Ezra recounts that, after the return from exile in Babylon, several men, among them priests and lay people, had taken foreign wives. This was a concern because it could draw the people away from their faithfulness to God. That is why the book records by family who acknowledged that wrong. This list is a record of those who agreed to correct their course. How that measure was carried out is a difficult question, and interpreters understand it in different ways.

God takes account of each person, by name and family. It also reminds us that acknowledging a fault openly and humbly is the first step toward correcting our direction. Today we can ask ourselves: is there something I should admit before God and before others in order to be faithful again?
exp.1:34:
This verse says that the descendants of Senaah who returned from exile numbered 3,630 people. It is part of a list of families and towns. The phrase "children of" does not always mean direct children; here it refers to the descendants or the group of a family or place. Scholars are not certain where Senaah was, and some believe it was a town or a clan.

The book of Ezra presents this list of the Jews who came back from Babylon to Judah, after the decree of King Cyrus. The narrator puts the numbers in writing to leave an orderly record of the people who returned. It mattered to know who belonged to each family, since this helped rebuild the life of the temple and of the community. This figure is the largest in the list, and the figures in Nehemiah 7 differ a little in other lists.

God knows and values every group and every person, even when no one mentions them in great stories. Today you can remember that your simple and steady service also counts in God's work. Give thanks for the ordinary people in your church.
exp.6:2:
This verse is part of a list of Ezra's ancestors. It names three people: Amariah, Azariah, and Meraioth (which appears here as "Meraioth"). Each is the son of the one that follows, so the list goes back in time until it reaches Aaron.

The author of the book, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra himself, though this is not certain, presents here the scribe's genealogy. He wants to show that Ezra came from a priestly family, a descendant of Aaron. That gave him authority and legitimacy before the people of Israel, just before he recounts his journey from Babylon to Jerusalem in the time of the Persian king Artaxerxes.

For today: God cares for people and for generations, even for those whose names almost no one remembers. Think of those who taught you the faith before you, and thank God for them. And remember that you too can be a link that passes that faith on to others.
exp.1:49:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned from exile in Babylon. It names three groups: the children of Asnah, of Mehunim, and of Nephusim. "Children" here means descendants, that is, whole families. The names are not well known. Some scholars think Mehunim and Nephusim may have been groups of foreign origin serving in the temple, but this is not certain.

Ezra, the scribe and traditional author of the book, carefully records who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. This section belongs to the temple servants, who helped with the tasks of worship. The list served to confirm who belonged to the people, and it took place during the rebuilding of the temple.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those no one remembers. Your humble and steady work in the church or in the family does not go unnoticed by Him. Serve faithfully, without seeking applause.
exp.7:17:
It says that God, with his good hand upon them, sent them help. A man of understanding came to them, a descendant of Mahli, who was from the family of Levi. Sherebiah also came, with his sons and brothers, eighteen people in all. The phrase about the good hand of God is a way of saying that God was watching over and favoring their journey.

Ezra, the priest and scribe, is speaking, and he was leading a group of Jews back to Jerusalem. He realized there were no Levites among them, and they were needed to serve in the temple. So he sent messengers to Iddo, at Casiphia, to ask for ministers. Ezra sees the hand of God in the answer.

Today we can learn to ask for help with humility and to act in faith. Ezra did his part, and then he recognized that God was the one who provided. When you face a need, do what you can and thank God for the people he places in your path.
exp.6:13:
This verse says that King Artaxerxes and his seven counselors sent Ezra to look into Judah and Jerusalem. Here, "to look into" means to examine and find out how things were going. He was to do this according to the law of God, which Ezra carried in his hand, meaning it was under his care and authority.

King Artaxerxes, the Persian king, is speaking in an official letter. The Jews had returned to their land, and the king gives Ezra permission, support, and resources. His seven counselors were his close advisers. The Bible does not explain why the king acted this way, but Ezra 7:6 and 7:9 say that the hand of God was upon him.

For today: carry the Word of God not only in your mind, but in your hand, that is, to live it out and let it guide your decisions. God can use even powerful people to open paths for those who obey him.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that 1,222 descendants of the family of Azgad returned to Judah. It is part of a list of families who came back from exile in Babylon. The phrase "children of" means descendants, not only direct children. The numbers appear as they do in the ancient text; in Nehemiah 7:17 the figure for Azgad is different (2,322), and it is not known for certain why. There are several possible explanations, such as copying errors or counts made at different times.

The book of Ezra, traditionally attributed to Ezra, tells of the return of God's people after about seventy years of exile. This list carefully records who returned with Zerubbabel, following the decree of King Cyrus. It showed that the people were still God's people, with their identity and inheritance.

For today: God knows his people, and he does not see anyone as a number without value. Even if your name does not appear in any important record, God knows you and calls you. Today you can thank him for this and value those who serve quietly beside you.
exp.3:17:
This verse says that the king received the letter from his officials and that it was read clearly in his presence. Some scholars believe that the word "clearly" may also mean "translated," because the letter was written in Aramaic, but this is understood in more than one way.

The speaker is King Artaxerxes of Persia. He is replying to Rehum and Shimshai, who had written against the Jews who were rebuilding Jerusalem. They accused the city of being rebellious. The king first confirms that he received and heard the report, and then orders an investigation.

For today: before believing an accusation against someone, it is wise to listen carefully and check the facts. The king did not act immediately but sent for a search. As Proverbs 18:13 says, answering before hearing is folly.
exp.9:18:
This verse tells that the priests mentioned promised with a solemn gesture, "gave their hands," that they would send away their foreign wives. They also presented a ram as an offering for their guilt, that is, a sacrifice to acknowledge that they had sinned.

The book does not name a narrator, although tradition connects it with Ezra. After the return from exile, the people had broken the law that forbade marrying peoples who worshiped other gods, because of the danger of turning away from God. The priests, who were meant to set an example, had also failed. This decision is harsh, and many readers debate it; the text presents it as an act of repentance in that historical moment, not as a rule for every marriage.

Today we can learn that truly repenting includes acknowledging the wrong, asking God for forgiveness, and changing what draws us away from Him, beginning with those who hold spiritual responsibility.
exp.2:0:
It says that when the seventh month had come, the Israelites who had returned from exile were already settled in their cities. Then all the people gathered together in Jerusalem, as one person, that is, with unity and one shared purpose. The word "come" in the verse is simply the sense of "when it came."

Here the narrator of the book of Ezra speaks. He tells what happened after the return from Babylon. The seventh month was very important in the law of Moses, because it brought sacred feasts, such as the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Tabernacles. The people gathered to worship, and the verses that follow show that the first thing they did was raise the altar, even though they feared their neighbors.

For today: when God comes first, unity becomes possible. Seek with your church or your family a regular time to worship together, even when there are fears or unfinished business.
exp.1:37:
This verse records that 1,247 descendants of Pashur returned to Judah. Pashur was one of the four families of priests listed here, along with Jedaiah, Immer, and Harim. The word "children" here means descendants or members of a family, not only direct children.

The author, traditionally identified with Ezra, writes a list of those who came back from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah after the decree of King Cyrus. The priests were essential for restoring worship in the temple. The exact numbers show that each family was counted carefully. This list also appears in Nehemiah 7, with small differences that scholars explain in various ways.

God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Every family and every name matters. Today we can serve faithfully in places that seem small, trusting that God values every contribution. No service done sincerely goes unnoticed by him.
exp.5:11:
The God who chose Jerusalem as the place for his name will destroy any king or people who tries to change this decree or tear down the temple. Darius states that he himself gave the order and asks that it be carried out quickly, with speed and diligence.

King Darius of Persia is speaking. Tatnai, governor of the region west of the Euphrates River, had questioned the permission to rebuild the temple. Darius searched out the decree of Cyrus, confirmed it, and ordered that the work be supported. This warning protects the project. It is remarkable that a foreign king speaks this way about the God of Israel.

For today: God can use even unexpected people to care for his work. When you face opposition in something God has placed on your heart, keep going with patience and obedience, and trust that he knows how to sustain it.
exp.5:17:
It says that, after the temple was dedicated, the priests and the Levites were placed in their groups for service to carry out the work of God in Jerusalem. The words "courses" and "divisions" refer to shifts or work assignments. Everything was done as it is written in the book of Moses.

The one telling the account is the author of the book of Ezra, which narrates the return of the Jews from exile in Babylon. With the temple finished, the people wanted worship to function in an orderly way and not by whatever idea came up at the moment. They relied on the Law of Moses. The exact details of how the shifts were arranged are understood in different ways, and the text does not explain them here.

For today: God is pleased with orderly and shared service. In your church or family, look for your place of service, carry it out faithfully, and let the Word of God guide how you serve.
exp.1:22:
This verse says that 128 men of Anathoth returned to Judea after the exile in Babylon. Anathoth was a small town near Jerusalem. The word "men" refers to men from that place, and here the count of how many returned is given.

The book of Ezra presents a list of the families and towns that returned with Zerubbabel, when the Persian king Cyrus allowed them to come back. It is not a speech but an orderly record of the people. It probably served to confirm who belonged to Israel and to divide the tasks of rebuilding the temple and the life of the people. Anathoth is also known as the hometown of the prophet Jeremiah, although this verse does not mention him.

For today: God does not overlook the small or the unnamed. Every person counted mattered in the rebuilding. You too have a place in what God is doing; serve faithfully where you are, even when no one applauds you.
exp.8:3:
This verse tells how several people who respected God's word came to Ezra because of the sin of those who had returned from exile. Ezra sat still, stunned and deeply troubled, until the time of the evening sacrifice.

Ezra was a priest and a teacher of the law. He learned that many Israelites, including leaders, had married people from the neighboring nations. The main concern was the danger that they would adopt those peoples' religious practices and turn away from God. Ezra felt deep sorrow and shame, and those who feared God gathered around him.

Today we can learn to feel genuine sorrow over sin, without treating it as unimportant. It is also good to stand together with people who respect God, and to bring our sadness to Him in prayer.
exp.5:0:
This verse says that King Darius ordered a search of the royal archives. They searched in the house of the rolls, that is, the place where documents and records were kept, along with the treasures of the kingdom, there in Babylon. The phrase "made a decree" means that he issued an order.

The account is told by the writer of Ezra. The Jews who had returned from exile were rebuilding the temple, but some opponents accused them before the king. They said Cyrus had authorized them, and Darius commanded that this be verified. The decree of Cyrus later turned up in another city, Ecbatana, which shows that the search continued beyond Babylon.

For today: when something you do in faith is questioned, do not despair. God can use the truth and documented facts to sustain his work. Act with honesty, trust in him, and be patient while he works.
exp.9:7:
This verse says that anyone who did not arrive in Jerusalem within three days would lose all their possessions and be cut off from the community of those who had come back from exile. The word "substance" in the verse means property, and the phrase about those who had been carried away refers to the exiles who had returned from Babylon. The word "separated" means excluded.

Ezra was deeply grieved because many of the people had married foreign women, and this was pulling them away from faithfulness to God. The princes and the elders agreed on this order to gather everyone together. Some scholars think that losing one's goods was a way of dedicating them to the temple; the text gives no further details.

For today: when we recognize a sin, we should respond quickly and with humility, without putting it off. God calls us to return to Him seriously, and to do so together with His people, not alone or in secret.
exp.1:14:
This verse says that from the family of Adin, four hundred fifty-four people returned. It is part of a list of families who came back to Judea after living in exile in Babylon. "The children of" does not refer only to direct sons, but to the descendants of an ancestor or of a family household.

The book of Ezra presents this list as a record of those who returned with Zerubbabel, after King Cyrus allowed them to come back. No speaker is named in this verse; the writer of the book, whom tradition usually identifies with Ezra, records the details carefully. The names and numbers are listed to show who made up the restored people. Interestingly, in Ezra 8:6 another family of Adin appears with a different number, and it is thought to correspond to another group that returned later.

For today: God does not see his people as an anonymous mass. Every family and every person counts. Serve others faithfully, even when your work seems small or no one sees it.
exp.7:10:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned to Jerusalem. It says that from the family of Bebai came Zechariah, son of Bebai, together with twenty-eight males. Here "males" means adult men, and the count probably includes those who could travel and work.

The book of Ezra presents Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law, who leads a second group of Jews from Babylon to Jerusalem, around 458 BC according to most scholars. He carefully records the names and numbers of the families, to show that God's people were returning in an orderly way and that each household had its place. Some details, such as the exact relationship between the heads of the families and the numbers, are explained in several different ways.

God looks at people, not only at crowds. Each name mattered, even if today it may seem like a dull list. Today we can remember that our service, though small and little seen, is valuable to God. You too have a place in his work.
exp.7:34:
It says that the Jews who returned from exile in Babylon, called "the children of the captivity" (those who had been carried away), presented offerings to God. The "burnt offerings" were sacrifices burned completely on the altar. They offered twelve bulls, ninety-six rams, and seventy-seven lambs. They also offered twelve male goats as a sin offering, that is, to ask forgiveness for sin.

Here the one telling the story is the narrator of the book, whom tradition usually identifies with Ezra. They had just arrived in Jerusalem after a long and dangerous journey, and had already handed over the treasures for the temple. The number twelve recalls the twelve tribes: they present themselves as one people before God.

For today: before beginning a new stage, stop to give thanks to God and to acknowledge your faults. A life that begins with gratitude and humility rests better on Him.
exp.5:2:
This verse recalls what an official document said: in the first year of his reign, King Cyrus ordered that the house of God in Jerusalem be rebuilt as a place for offering sacrifices. Its walls were to be firmly laid as foundations, and the building was to be sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, about half a meter, though its exact length is debated.

The neighboring peoples of the region had accused the Jews before King Darius to halt the work. Darius ordered a search of the archives, and in the city of Ecbatana (Achmetta) they found Cyrus's decree. This confirmed that the Jews had royal permission to rebuild the temple.

God can use documents, authorities, and even people who do not know him to carry out his plans. When you face opposition or delays, keep doing what is right with patience, and trust that God is still at work, even when you cannot see how.
exp.7:4:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that from the descendants of Shechaniah, the son of Jahaziel, three hundred males returned together with their leader. "Males" refers to adult men. Some older translations suggest that the name of the family was lost in the Hebrew text, so there is some uncertainty about that detail.

Ezra, the priest and scribe, records the names of those who came back with him from Babylon to Jerusalem. This was a second group of exiles returning to their land. Recording each family showed order, and also that God's people were real and had a history.

For today: God does not see faceless crowds but people with names. Your service, though it may seem small or little seen, counts in what God does among his people. Serve him faithfully and without comparing yourself to others.
exp.9:2:
Here Shechaniah proposes that the people make a covenant, that is, a solemn promise before God, to send away the foreign women and the children born of them. He says they will do it according to the counsel of the Lord and of those who tremble at his commandment, and according to the law.

Shechaniah, an Israelite, speaks after seeing Ezra pray and weep over the sin of the people. Many had taken wives from neighboring peoples, and the fear was that they would turn away from God and his law. It is a very painful decision. The Bible presents it here as an act of repentance, but many readers today find it difficult, and it should not be used to justify breaking up present-day marriages.

For today: when we recognize a mistake, let us seek God's direction in his Word and from wise counselors, and act with humility, not only with words.
exp.1:55:
This verse follows a list of families who returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. Three more names appear here: Jaalah, Darkon, and Giddel. They belong to the group called "the children of Solomon's servants," descendants of people who worked in the service of King Solomon. The ancient names do not tell us more details.

Ezra is the traditional author of the book, and here he records with care who returned with Zerubbabel. This list was important for rebuilding the community, organizing worship, and confirming which family each person belonged to. Scholars do not know much about these particular clans, but their presence shows that God took them into account.

God does not forget those who seem unimportant. Today we can serve faithfully in simple tasks, even when no one applauds us, trusting that the Lord sees and remembers every name and every effort.
exp.9:5:
It says that Ezra rose up from before the house of God and went into the room of Johanan, son of Eliashib. There he neither ate bread nor drank water, because he was deeply grieved by the wrongdoing of those who had come back from captivity. Wrongdoing here means betrayal or serious disobedience to God.

Ezra is the priest and teacher of the law. He had just learned that many Israelites had married women from neighboring peoples, which was drawing them away from God. He had already prayed and wept before the temple, and the people acknowledged their sin. Then the leaders swore to act. It is not known for certain whose room that was, but it was near the temple.

For today: when we see sin, even in our own community, we do not need to begin by judging harshly. We can grieve in our hearts, pray with humility, and seek to obey God with humility.
exp.9:28:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions six men from the family of Bani: Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal, and Ramoth. The phrase "sons of" refers to the descendants or members of that family.

We are in Ezra 10, after the return from exile in Babylon. The author, traditionally identified with Ezra, records who had married women from the neighboring peoples. This worried the leaders because of the risk of turning away from God, and the people committed themselves to correcting it. The list gives specific names to show that the matter was handled with order and responsibility. How that decision was carried out has been much debated, so it is worth reading it with care.

For today: God knows each person by name. He also invites us to honestly acknowledge our failures and to correct our course with humility.
exp.7:18:
This verse continues a list of people who joined the group returning to Jerusalem. It says that Hashabiah and Jeshaiah, descendants of Merari, one of the sons of Levi, also came. With them were their brothers and their sons, twenty men in all.

Ezra, the priest and scribe, speaks in the first person and recounts the journey from Babylon. He noticed that there were no Levites in the group, so he asked Iddo, at Casiphia, for help. These Levites and temple servants were needed for worship in the house of God. Ezra sees in this "the good hand of our God."

For today: God often cares for his work through ordinary people who serve faithfully, even when only their names are mentioned. We can ask ourselves in what humble place God invites us to serve, and do it gladly, without needing recognition.
exp.8:4:
He says that at the evening sacrifice Ezra rose up from his heaviness. His garments were already torn, so he fell on his knees and spread out his hands to God in prayer. "Heaviness" is his deep grief, and spreading out the hands was a common posture of prayer, with the hands opened toward heaven.

Ezra speaks here as a priest and teacher of the law. He has just learned that many of the people who returned from exile had mixed themselves with the neighboring peoples, following practices contrary to the law of God. He stays still, troubled, for hours. When the hour of the sacrifice comes, he leaves the silence and begins to pray, and in the verses that follow he confesses the sin of the people as if it were also his own.

For today: when something hurts you deeply, do not stay alone in the anguish. Bring it to God with humility and sincerity, and acknowledge whatever you need to acknowledge.
exp.1:18:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned from exile. It says that the descendants of Hasum, an ancestor or head of a family, numbered two hundred and twenty-three people. The phrase "the children of" does not always mean direct children; here it refers to the whole clan or family.

The book of Ezra has no narrator speaking in the first person in this part. The writer presents a record of those who returned from Babylon to Judah, after King Cyrus allowed the return. Counting each family showed that God's people were being rebuilt with order. It also helped establish who belonged to each community. Some figures in this list match Nehemiah 7 and others differ; scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: God takes notice of every family and every person, even those whom almost no one mentions. Today you can serve faithfully in your own place, though it may seem small, trusting that God sees it and values it.
exp.7:35:
Ezra and his companions delivered the king Artaxerxes' official letters to the governors and authorities of the region west of the Euphrates River. Sentences like these, written as a commentary on the wording itself, have no clear English equivalent, so the verse of the word itself is left out here. The authorities gave their help to the people and to the house of God.

Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law, tells of the return of a group of Jews from Babylon to Jerusalem. They had just delivered the treasures for the temple and offered sacrifices to God. Now the remaining formalities with the local authorities had to be completed. The text shows that this help arrived, and the context of the book suggests that God was also working through them.

Today we too can pray and act with order: complete the formalities and respect those in authority, trusting that God can move even those who do not know him to help with what belongs to him.
exp.9:21:
This verse is part of a list of names. It names six men from the family of Pashur: Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethaneel, Jozabad, and Elasah. They were of priestly descent, and each one is named individually.

Ezra 10 recounts a difficult moment after the return from exile in Babylon. The narrator tells that several men, including priests, had married women from neighboring peoples. Ezra saw this as a threat to the people's faithfulness to God, and it was agreed that they would separate from those women. This list records who was involved. Christians understand and apply this passage in different ways, and it is not easy. The text gives no further details about each case.

For today: God sees each person by name, and no one is hidden. Let us ask for humility to recognize our failings, especially if we are leaders, and for courage to correct our course with honesty.
exp.1:26:
It says that 122 men of Michmas, a town in the land of Benjamin, returned from exile in Babylon. The word "men" here simply means men, and the families are counted by their place of origin. Michmas was a small town north of Jerusalem.

The book of Ezra presents a list of the Jews who returned to Judah when Cyrus, king of Persia, allowed them to go back. No single character is speaking; the author, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, records the numbers in an orderly way. This showed who belonged to God's people and to which place they were returning. Some scholars note that other biblical lists have small differences in their figures, and it is not known for certain why.

For today: God overlooks no one, not even a small group from a little-known town. Your simple service and your faithfulness in everyday life also count for Him.
exp.9:10:
Tell the people to give honor to God by acknowledging their sin before Him. They should also do what God wants and separate themselves from the neighboring peoples and from the foreign women they had married. The phrase "give glory" means confessing humbly that God is right.

Ezra speaks after the return from exile, as a priest and teacher of the law. The men of Judah and Benjamin, gathered in Jerusalem in the rain, were trembling. Ezra tells them that they had married women from other peoples, and the text sees this as disobedience that put Israel's faithfulness to God at risk. The main reason the book gives is the danger of following other gods. Some scholars debate how this applies today.

When God shows us a mistake, the best thing is to acknowledge it sincerely and correct our course, without excuses. Today we can ask Him to help us remove whatever draws us away from Him.
exp.4:15:
Verse 16 says that Sheshbazzar came, laid the foundation of the house of God in Jerusalem, and from that time until now it has been under construction, yet it is not finished. The work kept moving forward from that moment, but it was still not complete.

The phrase "house of God" refers to the temple, and "Jerusalem" is the city of Jerusalem.

Tatnai, governor of the province west of the river Euphrates, and his companions speak in a letter to King Darius. The Jews had told them that King Cyrus had authorized the work, and they ask that the royal archive in Babylon be searched to confirm it. Some scholars think Sheshbazzar is the same person as Zerubbabel; others believe they are two different people.

For today: God can work through slow processes. Even when what He entrusted to you is not yet finished, do not lose heart; keep moving forward faithfully, one step at a time.
exp.3:13:
This verse says that the writers of the letter eat from the palace, meaning the king supports them and provides their food. That is why they say it did not seem right to them to see the king dishonored or harmed. The word "dishonour" means an offense or harm to his honor. So they informed the king of what was happening.

It was Rehum, Shimshai and their companions, officials of the Persian empire in the region. They write to King Artaxerxes to halt the rebuilding of Jerusalem. They say they do it out of loyalty, but they also protect their own position and their salary. Their accusations aim to frighten the king with the idea of rebellion and loss of revenue.

For today: when someone presents their actions as loyalty or righteousness, it is wise to ask about their real motives. And let us examine our own motives before opposing others.
exp.1:12:
It says that from the family of Adonikam, six hundred sixty and six people returned. It is part of a list of families who came back from exile in Babylon to Judah. "Children of" means descendants, not only direct sons.

The book of Ezra presents this list as an official record of the people who returned with Zerubbabel, after King Cyrus allowed them to come back. It is not certain who wrote the list, although tradition attributes it to Ezra. Also, Nehemiah 7 contains a similar list with some different figures, and scholars explain those differences in several ways. Here the aim is to show that God fulfilled his promise to restore his people.

Today it reminds us that God knows each family and each person by name. No simple service goes unnoticed by Him. You can serve faithfully where you are, even when no one else notices.
exp.7:14:
He says that Ezra gathered the people together by the river that runs toward Ahava, and that they stayed there three days in tents. When he looked over the people and the priests, he realized there was not one of the sons of Levi among them.

Ezra is speaking. He is the priest and teacher of the law who leads a group of Jewish exiles returning to Jerusalem from Babylon. Before setting out, he checks who is going. The Levites served in the temple and helped in worship, so their absence was a problem. For that reason, he later sends messengers to bring ministers for the house of God. The exact location of Ahava is not known for certain.

For today: before beginning an important project, take some time to check whether anything essential is missing. Ezra did not press ahead in a hurry; he stopped, evaluated, and sought what was needed to serve God well.
exp.6:20:
This verse says that King Artaxerxes gives an order to all the treasurers who are on the other side of the river (the region west of the Euphrates). Whatever Ezra the priest, scribe of the law of the God of heaven, asks of them, they must give it promptly, that is, right away and without delay. The words "It is commanded" mean that an order is given.

The speaker is the Persian king Artaxerxes, in an official letter he hands to Ezra. Ezra travels to Jerusalem with a group of Jews to teach the law of God and attend to the temple. The king gives him resources and authority. The verses that follow set limits on what is handed over, and the king says he does not want the wrath of the God of heaven to fall on his kingdom. Scholars do not agree on all of the king's political or religious motives, but the text shows that God can move rulers to help his people.

For today: trust that God can open paths and provision by unexpected means. Do your part faithfully and give thanks for those who help you.
exp.9:27:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that four men from the family of Bebai (Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai) were among those who had taken foreign wives. The phrase "sons of" refers to the members of a family or clan, not only direct children.

Ezra, a priest and teacher of the Law, tells how the people who returned from exile in Babylon had married women from neighboring peoples. The leaders recognized this and committed to correcting it. The list records the people involved by name. Interpreters debate how to apply this passage today, since the text focuses on the fear that the people would turn away from God.

For today: God values honesty. Acknowledging our failures by name, without hiding them, is the first step toward returning to Him. Ask yourself what area you need to name before God.
exp.9:42:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions seven men descended from Nebo: Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, Zebina, Jadau, Joel, and Benaiah. The phrase "had taken foreign wives" in the following verse explains why they appear: they were men who had married women from other peoples.

The book is written by a narrator, traditionally identified with Ezra. After the return from exile, Ezra learns that many Israelites had married women from neighboring peoples. He feared they would turn away from God, and the people publicly acknowledged their wrong. The list names each one, hiding no one. Scholars debate how to understand and apply this measure, and the text does not detail everything that happened to the families.

For today: God notices people by name, not anonymous crowds. This invites us to be honest, to acknowledge our failures with humility, and to seek to correct our course, trusting that God receives those who return to him sincerely.
exp.3:21:
This verse says that those in charge must take great care not to fail in this. The king asks why a growing harm should be allowed to develop, which, in his view, would hurt the kings, that is, their rule and their revenue.

It is King Artaxerxes of Persia speaking, in reply to a letter from his officials in Samaria who opposed the Jews. They accused Jerusalem of being rebellious. The king ordered the rebuilding to stop, and so the work on the temple halted for years, until the reign of Darius. This was a political decision based on accusations, not on the will of God.

Today we learn that persuasive accusations can stop good things. Before we act or judge, let us investigate with honesty. And if a good work is halted, God can resume it in his own time.
exp.2:1:
Verse 2 tells that Jeshua, the high priest, together with the other priests, and Zerubbabel, the leader of the people, with his companions, set to work. They built the altar of the God of Israel to offer burnt offerings, which were sacrifices burned completely in honor of God. They did this following what was written in the law of Moses, who is called "the man of God," that is, a man who belonged to God and spoke on His behalf.

The book of Ezra recounts the return of the Jews to Jerusalem after the exile in Babylon. No narrator speaks in the first person; the text simply reports the events. Before rebuilding the temple, the people, gathered in the seventh month, first restored worship. The verses that follow say they did so even though they were afraid of the neighboring peoples.

For today: before undertaking great projects, put God first. Even with fear, they obeyed and sought Him. You too can begin the day with prayer and the Word.
exp.9:25:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions six men from the family of Elam: Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi, Jeremoth, and Eliah. The names appear in the spelling used in the KJV above.

Ezra 10 tells that, after the return from exile in Babylon, some Israelites had married women from neighboring peoples. Ezra led the people in a time of repentance, and a list was made of those who acknowledged this wrong. The text gives no further details about each person. Scholars understand in various ways how this decision was applied, but the list shows that the matter was handled with seriousness and in a public way.

For today: God pays attention to people by name. It also reminds us that acknowledging a wrong in the sight of everyone, without hiding it, is part of returning to God with sincerity.
exp.1:25:
This verse records the descendants of two places, Ramah and Gaba, who returned from exile in Babylon: six hundred twenty-one in total. The phrase "the children of" means the inhabitants or original families of that place. Both towns were in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, very close to Jerusalem.

The writer of Ezra presents here a list of the families who returned with Zerubbabel, probably to show who made up the restored people. Scholars think this list served to confirm the identity of each family and its right to the land. An almost identical list appears in Nehemiah 7, with some differences in the figures.
