For today: God knows his people by families and places, not as an anonymous mass. Your faith and your service, though they may seem small, count for Him and for His work.
exp.1:4:
This verse says that seven hundred and seventy-five people from the family of Arah returned. "Children of Arah" means the descendants of one common ancestor, that is, a clan or family.

This list appears in the account that, according to tradition, was written by Ezra. It records the Israelites who came back from exile in Babylon to Judah and Jerusalem. They are listed by families to remember who they were and to rebuild the life of the people. In Nehemiah 7:10 the number for Arah is different (652). It is not known for certain why. It has been explained by copying errors, by counts made at different times, or by other reasons.

Today: God does not see his people as an anonymous mass. Even the less well-known families were recorded. Remember that your simple service and your name matter to God, even when no one else notices.
exp.1:60:
It says that three families of priests (the children of Habaiah, of Koz, and of Barzillai) returned from exile in Babylon. Barzillai married a daughter of another Barzillai, a Gileadite, and took the name of his father-in-law. "Was called after their name" means that he took on that family name. "Lineage" means the list of ancestors.

This is part of the list of those who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. The author, traditionally Ezra, carefully records who could prove their descent. The priests had to show that they came from Aaron. Since their record could not be found, these were set apart from the priesthood for a time, until the matter could be put before God. Scholars do not know for certain why his name changed.

For today: our identity before God does not depend on family names or titles, but on his calling and his grace. Even so, it is worth remembering that God values integrity and order in his service. Let us serve with humility and honesty.
exp.9:29:
This verse is part of a list of eight men, descendants of the family of Pahath-moab, who had taken foreign wives. "Sons of" here means members of that family clan. The names are recorded one by one, as in an official register.

Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law, keeps the record. After returning from exile in Babylon, the people had mixed their lives with the religious customs of the neighboring peoples. The leaders repented and committed to separating from those wives. It is a difficult scene, and today people debate how it should be applied, since the Bible also shows faithful foreign women, such as Ruth.

For today: God looks at each person, not only at crowds. Ask yourself honestly what influences draw your heart away from God, and ask Him for the courage to turn back with humility.
exp.7:8:
This verse records a group of families who returned from exile. It says that from the descendants of Joab, a man named Obadiah, son of Jehiel, was their leader, and 218 men traveled with him. The word "men" refers to adult men, probably heads of families or men of age to serve.

The author is the book of Ezra, which in this part seems to use the first-person account of Ezra, the priest and scribe. He led a second group of Jews from Babylon to Jerusalem, under the Persian king Artaxerxes. The list shows who they were, which families they came from, and how many there were. It is arranged by ancestral houses, something very important for Israel.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to names that almost no one remembers. Your humble and steady service also counts. Today you can take a step of faithfulness, knowing that God sees you and values you.
exp.9:31:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions three men: Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah. In the Bible, Benjamin here is the name of a person, not the tribe. The text says nothing more about them, only that they appear in the list.

Context: In Ezra 10, the people of Israel had returned from exile in Babylon. Many men, including priests and leaders, had married women from neighboring peoples who worshiped other gods. The people repented and decided to correct this. The writer, who according to tradition is Ezra, recorded the names of those who committed to doing so, so that there would be a record.

For today: God pays attention to people by name. Although these men barely appear elsewhere in the Bible, they were written down. Recognizing our mistakes and returning to God with sincerity has value, even when no one else notices.
exp.0:3:
This verse says that the Jews who had stayed in other lands were to be helped by their neighbors. They would be given silver, gold, goods, and animals for the journey. In addition, they could give freewill offerings for the temple in Jerusalem.

The word "goods" in the verse means possessions or property. The phrase "where he sojourneth" refers to the places where they lived as strangers. "Beasts" are the animals used to carry loads.

Speaking is Cyrus, king of Persia, in a decree that allowed the exiled Jews to return and rebuild the temple. This happened after the exile in Babylon. The text presents Cyrus acknowledging the God of heaven. Scholars debate what Cyrus truly believed, but the passage shows that God moved his decision.

For today: not all of us can go up to Jerusalem, that is, lead a work in front of others. But all of us can help with generosity and goodwill those who serve God. Think today of someone you can support with your time or your resources.
exp.0:4:
After the decree of King Cyrus, the leaders of the families of Judah and Benjamin, together with the priests and the Levites, set out. God stirred their spirit, that is, he put in their hearts the desire to return to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple. The family leaders are the heads of their households, and the word "go up" is used because Jerusalem sits on high ground.

The writer of the book tells this after the exile in Babylon. Cyrus, king of Persia, had allowed the Jews to return. Not everyone went back; those who felt God's call answered. The rest helped with offerings, as the context says.

For today: God still stirs the hearts of his people to serve him. If you feel the desire to do something good for his work, do not ignore it. Pray, take the step, and if you cannot go yourself, support those who can.
exp.0:9:
It says that, among the temple objects Cyrus returned, there were thirty gold bowls, four hundred and ten silver bowls, and a thousand other vessels. The "bowls" here are cups or containers used in worship. Note that the numbers in this inventory do not add up to the total in the following verse (5,400), and scholars explain this in several ways, for example, that some figures are approximate or that some objects were left out. There is no single certain explanation.

The author of the book, traditionally Ezra, carefully records what Cyrus handed over to Sheshbazzar, leader of Judah. The vessels had been taken from the temple by Nebuchadnezzar. Returning them showed that God was keeping his word and that worship in Jerusalem would be restored.

For today: God cares even for small details and does not forget what belongs to him. If you feel that something in your life was lost or carried far away, trust that God can restore it and use it again for his honor.
exp.7:6:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned to Jerusalem. It says that from the descendants of Elam, a man named Jeshaiah, son of Athaliah, led the group, and with him were seventy males.

The one speaking is Ezra, a priest and scribe, who tells of the journey from Babylon in the first person, around the time of King Artaxerxes of Persia. He records the names and numbers of each group with care, because he wanted to keep a record of who took part in this return and in the rebuilding of God's people. The names of Elam and others already appear in earlier lists of those who returned.

God takes note of people by name, not only of crowds. Today too, your service counts, even when it seems small or little seen. Serve faithfully where you are, because God remembers those who answer him.
exp.3:20:
This verse is part of King Artaxerxes' reply. He orders those men, the Jews who were rebuilding Jerusalem, to stop their work. The city must not be built any further until the king himself gives a new command.

Jerusalem's enemies had written to the king accusing the city of being a rebellious town. The king had the records searched and found that in the past Jerusalem had had powerful kings and had collected tribute. So he believed the accusation and halted the work. Notice that he left open the possibility of changing his decision later.

For today: not every obstacle means that God is opposing us. Sometimes accusations and unjust decisions bring a good work to a standstill. We can wait with patience, trusting that God is still at work.
exp.9:30:
This verse is part of a list of names. Five men from the family of Harim appear here: Eliezer, Ishijah, Malchiah, Shemaiah, and Shimeon. All of them are descendants of Harim, a clan that had already returned to Jerusalem after the exile. Some of these names are spelled differently in the version this explanation was written for, which is why the names are given here in the form your verse uses.

Ezra is the one leading the people, and the account tells the story in the third person. These men had taken foreign wives, and Ezra 9–10 explains that this was a concern because of the risk that the people would turn away from God. The list records, by name and family, those who agreed to correct that situation. How to apply this passage to other cases is understood in different ways, so it is wise to read it carefully.

For today: God looks at specific people, not at crowds. When He shows us something we need to correct, we can respond with humility and by name, without hiding among others.
exp.6:21:
This verse lists what King Artaxerxes authorizes to be given to Ezra from the royal treasuries: up to one hundred talents of silver, one hundred cors of wheat, one hundred baths of wine, one hundred baths of oil, and salt without limit. A talent was a large unit of weight, while the cor and the bath were units of volume: the cor for dry goods such as wheat, and the bath for liquids. Their exact equivalents are debated, but they were very generous amounts.

The king of Persia speaks in the letter he gives to Ezra, a priest and scribe, when he sends him to Jerusalem. The king wants the temple to have what is needed for worship, and he orders the treasurers beyond the river Euphrates to help Ezra. Ezra himself later acknowledges that God moved the king's heart.

For today: God can provide what is needed for his work in unexpected ways. We can pray with confidence, plan with responsibility, and give thanks for every help, whatever its source.
exp.0:7:
King Cyrus of Persia ordered the vessels of the house of the LORD to be brought out. He handed them over to Mithredath, his treasurer, who counted them out and gave them to Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah. "Brought out" means the vessels were taken out of storage; "by the hand of" means "through"; "numbered them" means that they were counted, one by one.

The author of the book tells how the exile in Babylon came to an end. Nebuchadnezzar had carried these vessels away from Jerusalem, and now Cyrus returns them so the temple can be rebuilt. Sheshbazzar appears as the leader of those who returned. Some think he is the same person as Zerubbabel, but this is not certain, and scholars discuss it.

For today: God cares about every detail and can use unexpected people to carry out his plans. You can trust that nothing that belongs to God is lost. It also encourages us to be faithful and orderly with what is entrusted to us.
exp.3:16:
This verse says that the king of Persia replied in writing to the officials who had written to him. He names them: Rehum, the chancellor (a high official), and Shimshai, the secretary (the scribe), together with their companions who lived in Samaria and in the rest of the region beyond the river, that is, west of the Euphrates River. The greeting "Peace" was a formal salutation, and the words that follow show that the letter continues.

Here King Artaxerxes responds. Rehum and Shimshai had written to halt the rebuilding of Jerusalem, accusing the city of being a rebellious town. The king ordered an investigation, and in the next verse he confirms that he found records of past rebellions. The texts do not say the accusations were fair; they were political pressure against God's people.

Today, when someone opposes the good you are doing with accusations or half-truths, do not lose heart right away. Pray, seek counsel, and keep trusting that God governs even when the authorities seem to be against you.
exp.9:35:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions Vaniah, Meremoth and Eliashib, men from the family of Bani. All of them are among those who had taken foreign wives.

Ezra is the one who leads the account, together with other leaders. After returning from exile in Babylon, some Israelites had married women from neighboring peoples who worshiped other gods. The people recognized their wrong and committed themselves to returning to God. The list records the names openly and in order, leaving no one out.

For today: God notices each person by name. If we have failed, he invites us to acknowledge it honestly and to return to him, hiding nothing. Doing so in humility opens the door to forgiveness and a new beginning.
exp.3:15:
Here the enemies of the Jews tell King Artaxerxes that, if Jerusalem is built up again with its walls finished, he will lose control of the region beyond the river, that is, the territory to the west of the Euphrates River. "Will be yours" means that it would no longer belong to him.

The speakers are Rehum, the chancellor, and Shimshai, the secretary, together with other officials from Samaria. They write a letter of accusation to stop the rebuilding. They claim to be loyal to the king, but their motives seem more like opposition and envy. They exaggerate the political danger, and the biblical text only records what they claimed.

For today: not everything that sounds like sincere concern is sincere. Before believing an accusation, it is wise to ask who is making it and what they stand to gain. And when you face unjust opposition for doing good, continue with humility and trust in God.
exp.7:28:
This verse says that the twelve priests in charge of the treasure were to guard it carefully until they reached Jerusalem. There they would weigh it before the chief priests, the Levites, and the heads of the families of Israel, in the chambers of the temple. "Watch" means to stay alert and careful. "Weigh" means to measure it on a scale. The "chambers" were the rooms or storerooms of the temple.

Ezra, the priest and teacher of the law, speaks during the return of the exiles from Babylon. He had set these men apart to carry the offerings from the king, his advisers, and the people. He reminds them that they and the objects are holy, dedicated to God. Weighing the treasure both when they left and when they arrived gave openness and prevented suspicion.

For today: what belongs to God deserves care, honesty, and clarity. If you manage money, time, or responsibilities in your church or family, do it with order and transparency, as one who is accountable before God and before others.
exp.7:30:
It says that the group left the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, heading toward Jerusalem. It tells us that the hand of God was with them, that is, that he took care of them and sustained them. God delivered them from enemies and from those who lay in wait, people who hid in order to attack by surprise. In this way they arrived safely along the road.

Ezra, a priest and scribe, speaks here, and he leads a group of Jews from Babylon back to Jerusalem. They carried silver, gold, and vessels for the temple. Earlier, he had decided not to ask the king for an escort, and he trusted in God (Ezra 8:22-23). This verse shows how God responded to that trust.

For today: God cares for us on the paths of life, even when we do not see the dangers. We can plan with wisdom and pray with confidence, and then thank him for his protection, including in the journeys of each day.
exp.9:38:
These three men are named: Shelemiah, Nathan, and Adaiah. They are part of a long list of names. Many ancient names carry the name of God within them, since names of this kind often mean something like "belonging to the Lord" or "of Jehovah."

The book of Ezra tells of the return of the Jewish people from Babylon. In this chapter, the scribe Ezra faces a problem: many men of the people, including families of priests and Levites, had married foreign women. The text presents this list as a record of those who agreed to set that situation right. How this measure should be understood and applied has been debated by interpreters, and it is a difficult passage. The author simply records their names.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom history hardly remembers. When we acknowledge a wrong and decide to return to God, our decision counts and stands before Him. Let us ask for the courage to correct what we must, with humility.
exp.1:50:
It says that some descendants of the families of Bakbuk, Hakupha and Harhur returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. They are part of a list of the temple servants and the descendants of Solomon's servants, people who served in the temple. The word "children" here means descendants or members of a clan, not necessarily direct children.

The book of Ezra is a historical account, traditionally attributed to Ezra, a priest and scribe. It records the census of those who returned to Jerusalem after the decree of King Cyrus. The list shows care in preserving the identity of the people and in organizing the rebuilding of the temple. Beyond these names we know almost nothing else, and their exact meaning is uncertain.

For today: God knows and remembers people whom no one else remembers. Your simple and hidden service also matters to Him. Serve Him faithfully, even when no one sees you.
exp.9:13:
This verse says that the leaders of the people would stay behind as representatives of the whole community. The men who had married foreign women would come at set times, along with the elders and judges of their city, to review each case. Note that "appointed times" is the phrase used in the verse itself. To break faith with a commitment means to have failed to keep a promise. The phrase about the fierce wrath of God refers to God's serious anger at that disobedience.

A group of the people speaks here, answering Ezra. After returning from exile, Ezra learned that many had married women from neighboring peoples, who practiced other religions. There was fear that they would turn away from the God of Israel. The people acknowledge their wrongdoing, but they ask for an orderly process, because there were many of them and it was the rainy season.

For today: when we recognize a wrong, it is good to act with humility and order, without excuses or haste. Let us seek help from wise people, and ask God for guidance to correct our course.
exp.1:54:
This verse begins a list of families who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. They are the descendants of the "servants of Solomon," that is, workers or attendants who served King Solomon. Three families are named here: Sotai, Sophereth, and Peruda.

Ezra, the scribe and priest, records this list to keep a written account of who returned with Zerubbabel. It was important to know who belonged to the people and who could serve in the temple. Not much is known about these groups; they are understood to have been families of foreign origin or of service, who over the years joined Israel. The exact details of their origin are not entirely clear.

For today: God remembers even the names that almost no one knows. Your service, though simple and quiet, does not go unnoticed before Him. Serve faithfully, without seeking applause.
exp.6:6:
This verse tells that along with Ezra went up to Jerusalem a group of people from the people of Israel: priests, Levites (those who assisted in the service of the temple), singers, gatekeepers (those who guarded the gates), and Nethinims (helpers of the temple, a group of servants). All of this happened in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes.

The one who narrates is the author of the book, who presents Ezra as a priest and scribe devoted to the law of Moses. Many believe that Ezra himself wrote or gathered this account, although the text does not state it here. The purpose is to show that the return from Babylon was ordered and that God accompanied Ezra, as the context says.

For today: serving God is not the task of one person alone. Ezra was the leader, but singers, gatekeepers, and helpers were also needed. Ask yourself what place you have in your church or community, and serve there faithfully, even when no one notices.
exp.9:36:
This verse gives only three names: Mattaniah, Mattenai, and Jaasau. They are part of a list of men from the family of Bani. The names appear in the form found in this verse, with their spelling as given in the text.

Context: The book of Ezra does not have a single speaker here; it is a narrative that lists names. After the return from exile in Babylon, Ezra discovered that many Israelites, including priests and leaders, had married women from neighboring peoples. This was seen as a danger to faithfulness to God. These men appear in the list of those who acknowledged their wrongdoing and committed themselves to correcting it. The list is a public and honest record. The situation was painful, and Christians understand it in different ways.

For today: God knows each person by name, including those whom history has almost forgotten. When we honestly acknowledge our failures, He gives us the opportunity to turn back to Him and start again.
exp.5:1:
After searching in Babylon without finding anything, they discovered a scroll in Achmetha, a fortress or palace in the province of the Medes. In it was written a "memorial," that is, an official record or note.

The Jews who were rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem had been accused by their neighbors, and the authorities doubted that they had permission. King Darius ordered the archives to be searched to verify whether Cyrus had really authorized the work. The account does not explain how that document came to Achmetha; it only says that it turned up there.

God can look after his promises even when everything seems lost or filed away somewhere far off. If you today face doubts or criticism for doing what is right, keep going with patience and trust that God knows how to bring to light what is needed at just the right moment.
exp.9:20:
This verse is part of a list of names. It names five men from the family of Harim: Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah. They were priests who had taken foreign wives. The phrase "gave their hand" means that they promised something with a formal commitment.

The book of Ezra tells of the return of the Jews from exile. Ezra, the priest and scribe, was distressed because some had taken wives from neighboring peoples, and he feared that this would turn them away from God. The narrator records here, by name, those who committed themselves to correcting this. How to understand this decision and its human consequences is something scholars debate.

For today: God pays attention to each person, not only to the crowds. When we recognize a fault, we can take concrete and honest steps to return to Him, without hiding who we are.
exp.8:0:
It says that, when certain tasks were finished, the leaders of the people went to Ezra with a serious complaint: the Israelites, including priests and Levites, had not separated themselves from the surrounding peoples. They had mixed with them and were following their detestable practices, that is, their idolatrous and wicked ways. "When these things were done" means "when all of that had ended." "Came to me" means "drew near to me."

The speaker is Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law who had returned from Babylon to Jerusalem. The leaders inform him that many had taken wives from those peoples. Ezra tells it in the first person. The concern was that Israel would lose its faithfulness to God, something the Law warned against (Deuteronomy 7:3-4). Some scholars point out that the problem was mainly religious, not ethnic.

Today we can ask ourselves what influences are shaping our faith. Living among other people with love is good, but we must take care that our loyalty to God does not weaken little by little.
exp.5:19:
This verse tells us that the priests and the Levites purified themselves together, and all of them were clean. Then they killed the Passover lamb for all the people who had come back from captivity, for their fellow priests, and for themselves.

The commentator notes that "together" means that they all acted at the same time.

The narrator of the book describes what happened when the temple was finished, rebuilt after the return from captivity. The people celebrated the Passover, which remembered the deliverance from Egypt. The priests and Levites had to be clean according to the law of Moses in order to serve in it. The king of Assyria is mentioned later; the text uses that title for the Persian king who supported the work, and some scholars explain this by Persian rule over former Assyrian lands.

Before serving others, we should let God cleanse our hearts. And it is a beautiful thing when God's people prepare themselves and worship together.
exp.6:7:
This verse says that Ezra arrived in Jerusalem in the fifth month of the seventh year of King Artaxerxes. The name of the city is written in an older form, Jerusalem, which is the same city we know today. The fifth month corresponds, more or less, to July or August on our calendar.

The author of the book tells the story in detail. Ezra was a scribe, that is, an expert in copying and teaching the law of Moses. He left Babylon with a group of Israelites, priests, and temple assistants. The following verse explains that the journey lasted about four months, and that they arrived safely because the good hand of God was upon him. This is mentioned to show that God watched over the way.

For today: Ezra prepared his heart before teaching and obeying. We can imitate him by giving steady time to reading the Bible sincerely, before wanting to guide others. And if there is a long road ahead of us, we can trust that God walks with us step by step.
exp.4:4:
This verse says that God watched over the leaders of the Jews, the elders. For this reason the governors did not force them to stop the work on the temple while the matter reached King Darius. "The matter" means the case or the issue. "But the eye of their God was upon the elders" means that God watched over them carefully and protected them. Meanwhile, the officials sent a reply to the king by letter.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, and in this part he tells what happened when the Jews who had returned from exile were rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem. Tatnai, a governor of the region, asked by what authority they were building. Instead of stopping them, he decided to consult King Darius.

For today: when you face opposition while doing what is right, keep going with patience and trust that God cares for you, even when you cannot see how the situation will be resolved.
exp.1:61:
These men claimed to be priests, but they searched the family records for proof of their descent and did not find it. For that reason they were set apart from the priesthood. The "genealogies" are the lists of ancestors.

This takes place in the account of those who returned from exile in Babylon. The author of the book, who records who could serve in the temple, is the one telling the story. The priesthood required descent from Aaron. The governor decided that they should wait until a priest could consult God by means of the Urim and the Thummim. It does not say what happened afterward.

Today we can be thankful that our place with God does not depend on papers or family. Jesus said that our names are written in heaven. Trust in his grace and serve with humility.
exp.1:40:
This verse says that among those who returned from exile in Babylon there were one hundred and twenty-eight singers. They were descendants of Asaph, a man who in the time of King David was in charge of the music in worship. The word "singers" refers to those who led the songs in the temple.

Ezra presents a list of the families who returned to Jerusalem around 538 BC, after the decree of King Cyrus. The author, traditionally Ezra, carefully records who came back: priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and other servants. In this way he shows that the people wanted to rebuild the temple and resume worship. It is notable that the singers were few compared with other groups, yet they were still recorded.

For today: God values gifts that seem small or quiet, such as singing in the congregation. Serve with what you have, without comparing yourself, because He takes note of every service done faithfully.
exp.9:37:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions Bani, Binnui and Shimei, men of Israel. The words are simple, but the list continues from one verse to the next. Only the people are named, with no further details about them.

Context: The book of Ezra does not present a voice speaking directly here; it is the account of the scribe Ezra. After the return from exile, some Israelites had married women from the neighboring peoples, and a record was made of those who committed to correct that situation. These names are part of that record. How to apply this episode today has been discussed at length, and it is worth reading it with care and humility.

For today: God knows people by their names, even when the story mentions them only in passing. Moreover, this record reminds us that honestly acknowledging our own mistakes, rather than hiding them, is the first step toward change.
exp.6:3:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that Ezra descended from Zerahiah, who was the son of Uzzi, and Uzzi in turn was the son of Bukki. These are links in a family chain that goes back until it reaches Aaron. The names appear in the old spelling of this version.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book, whom tradition usually identifies with Ezra himself, although this is debated. He presents the genealogy to show that Ezra came from a priestly family, a descendant of Aaron. This confirms that he had the right to teach and serve among the people who were returning from exile. It is probable that some names in the list have been left out, which is common in biblical genealogies.

God works through generations. We may not know our great-grandparents, but the faith we receive from others invites us to pass it on faithfully to those who come after us.
exp.6:16:
It says that Ezra is to use the money he has received quickly to buy animals for the sacrifice: young bulls (calves), rams, and lambs. He is also to buy the grain offerings and the drink offerings that went with them. Everything was to be offered on the altar of the temple in Jerusalem. The word "speedily" means "without delay."

The one speaking is the Persian king Artaxerxes, in an official letter addressed to Ezra, the priest and scribe. The king, together with his counselors, supports with money the worship of the God of Israel. The Jewish exiles had also given freewill offerings. Ezra was going to Jerusalem to teach God's law and to restore the service of the temple.

For today: what is given to God deserves careful attention and good order. If we handle church money or help for others, let us do it with honesty, fulfilling the purpose for which it was given.
exp.1:59:
The verse names three families: the children of Delaiah, the children of Tobiah, and the children of Nekoda, who together numbered 652 people. They were part of the group that returned to Judah after the exile in Babylon, but they could not prove with records that they were descended from Israel.

The book of Ezra presents a list of those who returned with Zerubbabel. The author, whom tradition identifies with Ezra, notes carefully who could prove their lineage. This mattered greatly for the life of the people and the service of the temple. The text does not say they were false Israelites, only that they did not have the register. Some think it may have been lost during the exile, but this is not stated.

God sees each person, even when others do not have their papers in order. These families appear in Scripture with name and number, and that reminds us that no one is anonymous to God. Today we can value those who do not have a brilliant record and welcome them with love.
exp.5:12:
It says that Tatnai, the governor of the region west of the Euphrates River, and Shethar-boznai, with their companions, obeyed right away what King Darius had ordered. The word "speedily" means quickly and without delay. The phrase "on this side the river" refers to the Persian province west of the Euphrates.

Earlier, these same officials had questioned the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem and wrote to the king to ask for guidance. Darius searched out Cyrus's decree, confirmed it, and ordered that the work be supported. Here we are told that they obeyed, and so opposition turned into help.

For today: God can work even through authorities who do not know Him. When He opens a door, our part is to respond with diligence and not leave the task unfinished. Trust Him when there are obstacles, and obey promptly when He shows you the next step.
exp.1:62:
It says the governor forbade certain men to eat from the most holy offerings, which were reserved for the priests. They would have to wait until a priest arose who could consult God by means of the Urim and Thummim. The Urim and Thummim were objects the priest used to learn the will of God; the Bible does not explain in detail how they worked.

The context is the return of the exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem. Some families who said they were priests could not find their genealogical record, so their right to the priesthood was in doubt. The governor, probably Zerubbabel, decided to wait for a clear answer from God rather than deciding hastily. Some believe Nehemiah uses the same title in another passage, but here that is not certain.

For today: when a decision is delicate and unclear, we should not rush. Let us seek God with humility, ask for wisdom, and act with care and respect for what is sacred.
exp.7:12:
This verse lists another group of families who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. The descendants of Adonikam are called "the last ones," that is, the final ones or those who came later. Three leaders are named: Eliphelet, Jeiel, and Shemaiah, and with them there were sixty men.

Ezra, the priest and scribe, is the one speaking, recounting how he gathered the exiles for the return. He records the family lists carefully because he wanted a well-ordered people, one that could rebuild its life around the temple and the law of God. Some understand "the last ones" to mean the final group of that family to return; the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: God takes notice of people by name, even in lists that may seem dull. Your service, though quiet or little noticed, matters. Be faithful in whatever God places before you.
exp.1:35:
This verse begins the list of the priests who returned from exile in Babylon. It says that 973 descendants of Jedaiah, of the family of Jeshua, returned to Judah. "The children of" means descendants, not necessarily direct sons. "The house of Jeshua" refers to the priestly family to which they belonged.

Ezra, the scribe and priest, compiles this record of the families who returned with Zerubbabel after the decree of King Cyrus. The priests were very important for rebuilding the temple and resuming worship. Scholars are not sure which Jeshua is meant here, nor of all the details of the list.

For today: God pays attention to every person, even when their name seems small. You also count in his work. Serve faithfully where you are, without comparing yourself to others, because God uses everyone to rebuild and restore.
exp.1:28:
This verse says that fifty-two descendants of Nebo returned from exile. "Children of" means the descendants of a family or the inhabitants of a town. Nebo here is probably a town in Judah, but it is not known for certain where it was. It should not be confused with Mount Nebo.

The author of the book, traditionally Ezra, copies the list of the Jews who returned from Babylon to Judea with Zerubbabel. This happened after the decree of King Cyrus, which allowed the temple to be rebuilt. The list shows that the return was real and ordered. It also shows that each family belonged to God's people.

For today: God overlooks no one, not even small groups. Your service may seem like a small thing, but God remembers it and uses it. Be faithful where you are, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.1:30:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned to Judah after the exile in Babylon. It says that the descendants of the other Elam numbered 1,254 people. It is called "the other Elam" because earlier, in verse 7, a family from Elam already appears with the same figure. We do not know for certain why the name and the number are repeated; some think they were two separate branches with the same name.

The book of Ezra presents this list as an official record, not as a speech. It tells how, under permission from the Persian king Cyrus, groups of Jews returned to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple. Recording each family showed that God was keeping his promise to restore his people.

For today: God does not see his people as an anonymous mass. Every family and every person counts for him. Today you can remember that your service, even when it seems small or hardly visible, has value in the work of God.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that the people were many, that it was the season of rains, and that they could not stand outside. Also, the matter would not be settled in one or two days, because many had broken faith, that is, they had failed in their commitment to God. The word for matter or case in this verse means business or affair.

The speaker is the people gathered in Jerusalem, answering Ezra. He had called them to repent of marrying foreign wives, which in that context carried the risk of turning away from God and his covenant. They accept the call, but ask for an orderly process, with leaders and set times, instead of a hasty decision in the open square.

For today: sincere repentance seeks to obey God, but it also needs order, patience, and humility. If there is something we must correct, let us not let it slide, even though it takes time. Let us ask God for wisdom and seek help from mature people in the faith.
exp.7:11:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned to Jerusalem. It says that from the descendants of Azgad a leader named Johanan, son of Hakkatan, returned, accompanied by one hundred and ten males. The word "males" refers to adult men, probably heads of families.

The writer is Ezra, who tells in the first person the journey from Babylon to Jerusalem, during the reign of Artaxerxes. Ezra notes carefully who was going with him, because he wanted to record that the people were returning organized, family by family. About the exact number of people, the list speaks only of males; we do not know for certain how many women and children accompanied them.

God counts people by name, each one specific. Johanan was not famous, but he was recorded. Your simple service, carried out faithfully in your family or church, also matters to God and does not go unnoticed.
exp.2:9:
This verse tells that, when the builders began to lay the foundations of the temple, the priests came forward in their special clothing and with trumpets. The Levites, descendants of Asaph, played cymbals (metal plates). All of them praised the Lord, following the order that King David had left for worship. The builders are the workers who laid the stones, and the word "ordinance" in the verse refers to the established instruction that David had set down.

The author is the scribe who records the return of the Jews from exile in Babylon. Zerubbabel and Jeshua led the rebuilding. Before seeing the temple finished, they wanted to celebrate God for the first step. Afterward, the text says that some of the elders wept as they remembered the earlier temple, while others shouted for joy.

Today we can praise God from the beginning of a project, without waiting to see it finished. Give thanks for the first steps, even when they are small.
exp.0:10:
It says that in total there were five thousand four hundred vessels of gold and silver, that is, articles used in the temple. Sheshbazzar brought them up to Jerusalem along with those who were returning from the captivity in Babylon.

The author of the book (tradition links it to Ezra, though this is not certain) tells how King Cyrus allowed the Jews to return and gave back what Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple. Sheshbazzar was a leader of Judah; some believe he is the same person as Zerubbabel, but this is not known for certain. The figures in the list before this verse do not add up to 5,400, and this is explained in different ways, for example, that the list is partial.

God does not forget what belongs to Him. Even after years of loss, He cared for every detail to restore worship. Trust that He can also restore what seemed lost in your life, and faithfully care for what has been entrusted to you.
exp.1:48:
This verse names three families: the descendants of Uzza, of Paseah, and of Besai. It is part of a long list. "Children of" here means descendants or members of a clan, not only direct sons.

The passage is part of the record of the Israelites who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem after the exile. These families appear among the temple servants (from verse 43 onward). The writer, traditionally thought to be Ezra, wants to keep a record of who returned to rebuild the life of the people and their worship. The exact origin of these temple servants is not entirely certain.

For today: God does not forget those who serve in small ways and without applause. These almost unknown names were written down. Serve faithfully wherever you are, even when no one notices; God does see it.
exp.1:2:
This verse opens the list of the families who returned from exile. It says that from the family of Parosh, two thousand one hundred and seventy-two people came back. "Children of" means descendants, that is, members of the same clan. Parosh was the largest family in the list.

The text is an official list, written by a narrator who copies a record kept by the people. After about seventy years in Babylon, the Israelites returned to Judah under the leadership of Zerubbabel and Jeshua. Counting each family helped people recognize who belonged to the people and how the land would be divided. Some scholars think the list differs from the one in Nehemiah 7, and there is no single certain explanation for this.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Every family and every person counts. Your service, even if it seems small or little noticed, is held in God's memory. Offer him today what you can do with faithfulness.
exp.9:23:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that among the singers Eliashib was found, and among the gatekeepers of the temple Shallum, Telem, and Uri. The gatekeepers were the men responsible for watching over the doors of the house of God.

The book of Ezra does not let any character speak here; it is the narrative that lists these men. After the return from exile, Ezra learned that many Israelites, including priests and temple servants, had married women from neighboring peoples. It was feared that this would draw them away from God. That is why their names are recorded, although the list does not explain each case, and scholars debate how this measure should be understood and applied.

For today: God pays attention to people by name, and he expects honesty from those who serve in his house. If there is something in your life that pulls you away from God, acknowledge it with humility and ask him for help to correct it.
exp.9:33:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions three men from the family of Bani: Maadai, Amram, and Uel. It forms part of a longer record of people who had taken foreign wives. The phrase "sons of" here means descendants or members of that family.

The book of Ezra is traditionally attributed to Ezra, a priest and scribe, although the text sometimes speaks of him in the third person. After the return from exile, the people had become mixed with neighboring nations who worshiped other gods. The leaders acknowledged their wrongdoing and recorded the names of those involved. How the solution they adopted should be understood is something readers debate, since it is a difficult passage.

God takes account of each person, by name. It also reminds us that sincerity calls for acknowledging our mistakes honestly and without hiding. Today we can ask ourselves what we need to admit before God, and take a concrete step of change.
exp.8:5:
Here Ezra prays to God and says he is so ashamed that he can hardly bring himself to look up to him. He is covered with shame, and the wrongs his people have done weigh heavily on him. Ezra's words picture the sins as piling up high over his head and reaching all the way to heaven, which shows that the sin is very great and that God sees it.

Ezra speaks as a priest and teacher of the law, after returning from exile in Babylon. He had learned that many of the people, including leaders, had married women from neighboring nations who worshiped other gods, which the law of Moses forbade because it risked turning the people away from God. Ezra does not accuse others. In his prayer he speaks of "our" iniquities, and he identifies himself with the people.

For today: when we fail, instead of making excuses or pointing at others, we can come before God with humility and honesty. He receives with mercy the one who acknowledges his sin.
exp.8:7:
He says that God, for a brief moment, showed mercy to his people: he let a small group survive and return, gave them a "nail" (a firm and secure place, like a tent peg driven deep into the ground) in his sanctuary, and gave them new hope, to "lighten our eyes," and a little relief in the midst of their bondage.

Ezra speaks this prayer after learning that many Jews who had returned from exile had mixed with the customs of the neighboring peoples and disobeyed God. He acknowledges the people's guilt and recalls that, even so, God had shown them kindness by allowing them to return and rebuild the temple.

For today: when you fail, do not dwell only on your guilt. Remember the times God has given you grace, and let that kindness lead you to repent sincerely and return to obeying him.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that 945 people from the family of Zattu returned to Judah. It is part of a list of families who came back from exile in Babylon. "Children of" here means descendants or members of a clan, not only direct sons.

Ezra 2 is a record of those who returned to Jerusalem and Judah after King Cyrus allowed the Jews to go back. The author, traditionally Ezra, notes family by family. This served to show the identity of the people, their heritage, and their right to live in the land. Some numbers differ a little in Nehemiah 7, and scholars explain this in different ways, with no single certain answer.

For today: God looks at each family and each person, even when we are not famous. Being part of his people does not depend on being notable, but on responding to his call. Today you can ask yourself how to serve faithfully in your place, with steadiness, knowing that God sees and remembers your effort.
exp.9:16:
This verse says that the group in charge finished reviewing the cases of all the men who had married foreign women. They finished on the first day of the first month, that is, three months after they had begun on the first day of the tenth month. "They made an end" means they completed the investigation.

It is part of the account of Ezra, who led the people after returning from exile. They were concerned that these marriages would lead them to worship other gods, as had happened before. The text does not give every personal detail of each case, and today people debate how this very harsh measure should be understood.

For today: God values processes carried out with order and patience. When you need to correct something important in your life or family, do not rush; investigate carefully, seek counsel, and act with humility and truth.
exp.7:15:
Here Ezra tells how he sent for eleven trusted men. Nine are called "chief men," that is, leaders of the people, and two are men of understanding, meaning people with insight and wisdom. The word "sent" here is the same as "sent" in the verse. The names repeat a little (several are named Elnathan), and we do not know for certain whether they are different people or whether some details were lost in copying.

Ezra speaks in the first person. He had gathered a group of Jews by the river Ahava to return to Jerusalem, but he noticed that there were no Levites, the men responsible for service in the temple. So he sent these men to ask Iddo for help, to obtain ministers for the house of God.

For today: when something important is missing in the service of God, it is not enough to notice it. It is wise to act in an orderly way, to pray, and to seek out capable people who are willing to help.
exp.7:13:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem. It says that from the family of Bigvai, two leaders went back, Uthai and Zabbud, and with them seventy males. Here, "males" refers to adult men, probably heads of families or people old enough to travel.

The one speaking is Ezra, a priest and teacher of God's law. He leads a second group of Israelites from Babylon, under the permission of King Artaxerxes. He records the names and numbers carefully because every family mattered among God's people. The details show that it was an organized and real return, with specific people.

For today: God knows people by name, even those who pass almost unnoticed. You can serve faithfully in simple things, and also value and thank those who work without applause in your church or family.
exp.6:24:
God told Ezra that he gave him wisdom, and that with it he was to appoint judges and governors for the people on the other side of the river (the Euphrates, the region to the west). They would govern those who already knew God's laws, and Ezra and his companions would teach those laws to those who did not know them.

The speaker is the Persian king Artaxerxes, in an official letter he gives to Ezra, a priest and scribe. The king supports the rebuilding of worship in Jerusalem and gives Ezra civil and religious authority. Scholars debate how far that authority extended, but the text shows that God's law was to be known and taught.

For today: justice and leadership need God's wisdom and patient teaching. If you lead in your home, church, or workplace, do not only correct; teach clearly and with love to those who do not yet know.
exp.6:22:
It says that whatever the God of heaven commands for his temple must be done with diligence. The king asks why God would be angry with his kingdom and with his sons, that is, with his family and his heirs. It is a way of saying: let us carry this out so as not to provoke his anger.

The speaker is the Persian king Artaxerxes, in a letter he gives to Ezra, priest and scribe of the law. He orders his treasurers to give silver, wheat, wine, oil and salt for the temple in Jerusalem. We do not know for certain what the king personally believed; his language may have mixed sincere respect with political interest. Even so, the book shows God's hand moving his heart.

Today, when we know what God wants, let us obey without putting it off. A concrete step: do today what we have left pending.
exp.4:10:
They answer the Persian officials with humility: they present themselves as servants of the God of heaven and earth. They explain that they are not building something new, but rebuilding the temple that had been built many years ago by a great king of Israel, whom almost everyone understands to be Solomon.

The speakers are the elders of the Jews who had returned from exile. Tatnai, the Persian governor, asks them by what authority they are building and writes a letter to King Darius. The Jews do not defend themselves with pride; they explain who they are, whom they serve, and why they are working on the temple.

For today: when someone asks you why you do what you do, answer with simplicity and respect, without showing off. Your identity as a servant of God can guide your work and your words. And if something good in your life has been ruined, God can help you rebuild it.
exp.2:12:
It says that, when the foundations of the temple were laid, there was so much shouting that no one could tell which sound was joy and which was weeping. The word "discern" means to tell apart. "Jubilation" is a very great joy. The phrase "could be heard" simply means it could be heard. The mixed noise carried a long way.

The book of Ezra does not say with complete certainty who wrote it; tradition connects it with Ezra. It tells of the return of the Jews from exile in Babylon. The young people celebrated the new work. The elders, who had seen the first temple, wept, probably over what had been lost, and perhaps because this new temple seemed more modest. The text does not explain their reasons, so this is a common interpretation.

Today we can learn that joy and sorrow can live together in the heart. God receives both our gratitude and our pain. We can praise him for the new thing he is doing, without being ashamed to weep over what has passed.
exp.6:25:
This verse says that whoever does not keep the law of the God of Ezra or the law of the king will be judged without delay. The punishment could be death, banishment (being sent away or cut off from the community, though some understand it as exclusion), a fine that took away one's property, or prison.

The speaker is the Persian king Artaxerxes, in an official letter given to Ezra. He grants Ezra authority to appoint judges and enforce the law in the region west of the Euphrates River. The Persians usually supported the religious customs of the peoples in their empire, and so Ezra could direct the life of the Jewish people. Ezra then praises God for having moved the king's heart.

For today: obedience to God is not decoration but something serious. We can ask him to help us live with integrity, keeping his Word and also respecting the just laws of our country.
exp.1:19:
This verse is part of a list and says that ninety-five descendants of Gibbar returned from exile. "The children of" here does not mean only direct sons and daughters, but members of a family or clan. Some older translations read "Gibeon" in the parallel text of Nehemiah 7:25, so the name may have been written or understood in different ways.

The book of Ezra records the Jews who came back from Babylon to Judah after the decree of King Cyrus. No character speaks in this verse; it is the writer's account, carefully noting names and numbers. The list shows that the return was real, organized, and made up of specific families, and that each group had its place among God's people.

For today: God does not see His people as an unnamed crowd. Even a small group was recorded. You can trust that your simple service and your faithfulness also matter to Him. Today, value and thank someone whose work almost no one notices.
exp.3:3:
This verse says that the people who lived in the land discouraged the Jews and took away their strength. The phrase "weakened the hands" means to drain away courage and resolve. "Troubled them" means to frighten them or push them back, so that they would stop building the temple.

The narrator then describes what happened after Zerubbabel and the leaders turned down the help of their neighbors. Those peoples had been brought there by the Assyrians, and they said they worshiped the same God, though not all of them understood him in the same way. The Jews answered that King Cyrus had entrusted the work to them. Once they were refused, the neighbors began to pressure them and oppose them.

For today: when doing what is right brings opposition or discouragement, you are not alone. Ask God for strength, surround yourself with people who encourage you, and keep going with what He has entrusted to you, even when progress is slow.
exp.9:14:
This verse names four men: Jonathan, Jahaziah, Meshullam, and Shabbethai. Two were put in charge of the matter, and two Levites helped them. Some translators understand that Jonathan and Jahaziah opposed the plan, because the Hebrew verb can carry both meanings.

Ezra was leading the people of Judah after their return from exile. Many had married foreign women, and Ezra saw this as unfaithfulness to God. The people asked for an orderly process, with time and with leaders, because there were many of them and it was raining.

For today: when a serious wrong needs correcting, let us do it with order, patience, and the help of others, not in a rush or alone. And if someone thinks differently, let us listen with humility.
exp.4:3:
The verse says that the Jews answered the Persian officials by giving them, one by one, the names of the men who were leading the construction of the temple. The phrase "in an orderly manner" means they did it in a systematic way, hiding nothing. "They were building this building" refers to the rebuilding of God's house in Jerusalem.

The speaker is a group that includes the writer of the letter, in the part of the book written in Aramaic. Tatnai, governor of the province west of the Euphrates River, came to investigate by what authority the temple was being raised. The Jews did not hide themselves: they gave the names clearly, knowing they were answering to an authority.

For today: when your faith or your work is questioned, you can respond with openness and order, without fear. Whoever acts with integrity and trusts that God cares for his work can face the question with calm.
exp.9:22:
This verse lists six men from the tribe of Levi: Jozabad, Shimei, Kelaiah (also called Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer. They were Levites, that is, descendants of Levi, who were responsible for service in the temple. The phrase "also called Kelita" indicates that Kelaiah was another name for the same man.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, identifying himself as Ezra. After the return from exile, many Israelites, including priests and Levites, had married women from neighboring peoples. Ezra called them to acknowledge their wrongdoing. This list records by name who did so. Scholars understand the list as a record of those who committed to sending away their foreign wives; it is a difficult and debated subject.

For today: those who serve God should live with honesty, acknowledging their mistakes without hiding them and seeking to correct course with humility.
exp.1:21:
This verse says that 56 men from Netophah returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. The word "men" here is the one used in the verse itself, and Netophah was a town near Bethlehem. The verse counts men here where another wording might count sons, but the idea is the same: it records the families or inhabitants of that town.

Ezra 2 is an official list of those who returned with Zerubbabel after the exile. No one is speaking in it; the author, traditionally Ezra, records names and numbers to show that God kept his promise to bring his people back home. This list also helped organize the life of the people, their worship, and their land.

For today: God does not overlook small people or small groups. Fifty-six men from a modest town were recorded. If you feel unimportant, remember that God sees you and values your part in what He is doing.
exp.3:2:
Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the other leaders of Israel's families reject the offer of help. They say it is not right for them to build the temple together with these people. They alone will build it for the Lord, the God of Israel, because King Cyrus commanded it. The phrase about the heads of families means the leaders of each household, and the phrase about it not being right for them means that the work does not belong to those people.

The speakers are the Jewish leaders who returned from exile. Their neighbors called themselves worshipers of God, but they were people brought in from Assyria, and the Bible suggests that their faith was mixed with other practices. The leaders look after the work and obey the king's order. Their answer provoked opposition, although some scholars debate how sincere the offer was.

We can be kind to everyone and still carefully guard what God has entrusted to us. Before accepting a partnership, it is wise to pray and ask whether it helps us obey God.
exp.9:15:
This verse tells that the people who had returned from exile carried out the plan they had agreed upon. Ezra the priest and some heads of families, named one by one, were set apart for this task. On the first day of the tenth month they sat down to look into the matter carefully and investigate the case.

The book of Ezra tells the story of the people's spiritual rebuilding after the exile. Many Israelites had married women from neighboring peoples, and Ezra saw this as a danger to faithfulness to God. The assembly agreed to examine each case in an orderly way. Some readers see here a zeal for the purity of the faith; others point out how painful these separations were.

For today: when something serious needs correcting, it is good to do it with prayer, order and humility, listening and examining the facts calmly, and not in haste or anger.
exp.1:45:
This verse is part of a list of families. It names three groups: the children of Hagab, of Shalmai, and of Hanan. "Children" here means descendants, that is, whole families. They were among the temple servants, called Nethinim in verse 43. No story is told about these families; only their names appear.

Ezra records who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. No character is speaking in this passage; it is a written record by the author. His purpose was to keep a record of the families who came back to rebuild the temple and the life of the people. Names in lists like this are sometimes spelled in different ways, and their exact meaning is uncertain.

For today: God sees and remembers the people no one else mentions. If your service is quiet and unseen, do not belittle it. Serve faithfully, because God knows your name.
exp.1:47:
This verse is part of a list of families. It names the "children" of Rezin, of Nekoda and of Gazzam, that is, their descendants. Here "children" means families or clans, not only direct sons and daughters. These groups belonged to the Nethinim, who were servants of the temple.

Ezra does not speak here as in a sermon; the book lists those who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem, around 538 B.C. The list shows that the return was orderly and that each group mattered. The Nethinim helped the Levites in temple tasks. Scholars hold different ideas about their origin, and nothing can be stated with certainty.

For today: God knows names that we would overlook. Your service, even when it is simple and quiet, matters to Him. Serve faithfully, without seeking applause.
exp.4:13:
It says that Nebuchadnezzar took the gold and silver vessels from the temple in Jerusalem and placed them in the temple of his god in Babylon. Later, King Cyrus removed them from there and handed them over to Sheshbazzar, whom he had appointed governor. The phrase "were delivered" means that they were given to him so that he could carry them back.

Here the Jewish leaders are speaking, answering the governor Tatnai, who asked them by what authority they were rebuilding the temple. They cite Cyrus's decree as proof. As for who Sheshbazzar was, there is debate: some think he is Zerubbabel under another name, and others think they are two different people.

God took care of what seemed lost forever. Those sacred objects returned to their place when the time came. If today you feel that something valuable in your life or your faith has been lost or left in other hands, trust that God can restore it, and in the meantime remain faithful with what you still have in front of you.
exp.1:3:
This verse says that a group of families, the descendants of Shephatiah, returned from exile in Babylon, and that they numbered 372 people.

This is part of an official list of those who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, after about seventy years of exile. There is no narrator speaking to anyone in particular; the author, traditionally Ezra, records the names and the figures. He does this to show that God kept his promise to restore his people and to identify the true heirs of the land and the temple. The figures in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 sometimes differ, and this is explained in several ways.

For today: God knows and counts every family, even a small one. You are not a lost number; serve faithfully where you are.
exp.5:18:
This verse says that the Jews who had returned from exile in Babylon kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month. The word "captivity" refers to the exile, that is, the time when they had been taken far away and were now returning to their land.

The one who records this is the author of the book of Ezra, which tells of the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem. They had only just dedicated the house of God, and the first thing they did was keep the Passover, the feast that remembered how God delivered them from Egypt. In this they followed what was written in the law of Moses. Since they were now purified, they could worship with a clean and thankful heart.

For today: after a difficult time, do not forget to remember what God has done for you. Recalling his faithfulness and putting it first renews your gratitude and draws you close to him again.
exp.4:1:
It says that Zerubbabel, who was the governor of Judah, and Jeshua, the high priest, set out and began to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah were with them and were supporting them. "Rose up" means that they made the decision to act. "Build" means to construct.

The narrator is the author of Ezra, who tells what happened when the Jews returned from exile. The work on the temple had stopped because of opposition from their neighbors. God sent Haggai and Zechariah to encourage the people, and then they resumed the work. Shortly afterward, the Persian authorities came to ask under whose permission they were building.

For today: when a good task that God placed in your heart has stopped because of fear or weariness, start again. Do it with brothers and sisters who encourage you with the Word, and not alone.
exp.1:51:
This verse is part of a list of families. It names the children of Bazluth, of Mehida, and of Harsha, which were groups of descendants who returned to Jerusalem. The phrase "the children of" means "the descendants of," that is, whole families or clans.

The book of Ezra tells of the return of the Jews after the exile in Babylon. The author, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra, though this is not absolutely certain, carefully records who returned. These people belonged to those called "temple servants," servants of the temple. Of many of these names we know very little, and their exact meaning is uncertain.

For today: God knows and remembers the people who serve quietly. None of them were famous, yet their names were written down. If your work in the church or at home goes unnoticed, take heart: nothing you do for God is forgotten by Him.
exp.1:64:
It says that, in addition to the 42,360 people who came back from exile, there were 7,337 male and female servants, and also 200 male and female singers. The word "beside" here means "not counting," that is, "in addition to." The servants were people who worked in the service of families.

This is part of the list of Jews who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem, around 538 B.C. The text is a recorded narrative, not a speech. Even small details are noted, such as the singers and the animals, to show that the people were restored in an orderly way. The numbers in this list and those in Nehemiah 7 do not match exactly, and several explanations have been proposed, but it is not known with certainty which one is correct.

God takes account of every person, even those whom almost no one notices. Today you can value and thank others for their service and their praise in your church, and also offer your own contribution with joy.
exp.1:20:
This verse says that 123 descendants of families from Bethlehem returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. The phrase "the children of" means descendants or relatives of a place or of an ancestor. It is part of a list of people counted by family or town.

Ezra, a scribe and priest, records this list to show who returned with Zerubbabel after the exile. It was important to note each group in order to rebuild the people, the temple, and life in the land. Bethlehem appears here as a small town, and nothing in this verse says more about its future. Later biblical texts mention it in a special way, but here only its people are counted.

For today: God takes persons into account one by one, even when they seem few or little known. You can serve faithfully in your place, without comparing yourself, trusting that God values your part in what he is building.
exp.3:9:
This verse continues the list of those who signed the letter. It says that the other peoples whom the great and noble Asnappar brought over and settled in the cities of Samaria also wrote, along with other inhabitants of the territory west of the river Euphrates. "Brought over" means that he carried them by force from one place to another. "And so forth" indicates that the list is summarized and not written out in full.

The speakers are Rehum, Shimshai and their companions, who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem. They write to the Persian king to accuse the Jews. Asnappar probably refers to an Assyrian king who moved populations, though it is not known for certain who he was. Scholars interpret him in several ways.

For today: opposition sometimes gathers together and looks very numerous, but that does not make it just. If God calls you to a good work, do not lose heart because of the voices against you. Pray, keep going with humility, and trust that God sustains what he has begun.
exp.1:9:
This verse says that 642 descendants of the family of Bani returned to Judea. "Children of" does not mean only direct sons, but a whole family or clan that came from one common ancestor.

This is part of a list of the Jews who returned to their land after the exile in Babylon. The book of Ezra, which tradition attributes to Ezra, keeps these records to show that God fulfilled His promise to bring His people back. Nehemiah 7:15 gives a different number for this family, and we do not know the reason for certain. Some think lists from different moments were used.

For today: God knows each family and each person by name. No one is a mere number to Him. You can rest in the knowledge that God sees you, remembers you, and includes you in His work.
exp.8:2:
Ezra tells that, upon hearing the report about the mixed marriages, he tore his clothes, pulled out hair from his head and beard, and sat down stunned, that is, paralyzed by the shock and the pain. The outer garment was the cloak. These gestures were signs of mourning and deep distress.

Ezra speaks as a priest and teacher of the law, after the return from Babylon. The leaders inform him that many of the people, including priests and rulers, had married people from the neighboring nations. The central problem was the danger of falling into their idolatrous practices (detestable things). Ezra does not react with cold anger, but with grief and humility, and then he prays.

For today: when you see sin around you, do not take it with indifference or with pride. Let it grieve you, bring it to God in prayer, and seek to correct it with humility, beginning with your own heart.
exp.7:1:
This verse begins the list of the heads of family who returned from Babylon. It names three: Gershom, a descendant of Phinehas (from a priestly family); Daniel, a descendant of Ithamar (also of priestly lineage); and Hattush, a descendant of David. Here "sons" means descendants, and the spelling of Phinehas and Ithamar in the verse is the same as in the verse's source.

The speaker is Ezra, a priest and scribe. He tells how he left Babylon with a group of Jews during the reign of Artaxerxes. He records the names to show who these people were and which families they came from. In this way the identity of the people and the service in the temple were cared for. It is not known with certainty whether this Hattush is the same person mentioned in other passages.

For today: God knows each person by name, even when someone seems to be just a name in a list. Remember that your service, however small it may seem, matters to God.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that a group of families called "the children of Pahath-moab" returned from exile, and that there were 2,812 of them. It notes that they were descended from Jeshua and Joab. The phrase "the children of" means descendants or members of a clan. The name Pahath-moab may mean "governor of Moab," but its exact origin is uncertain.

This is part of a list of the Jews who came back from Babylon to Judah after King Cyrus allowed them to return. The text is a careful record, written to identify each family and its place among the restored people. Scholars are not sure who this Jeshua and this Joab were exactly; they could be ancestors of the clan or leaders of branches of the family.

For today: God forgets no one, and every person counts in his work. Serve faithfully wherever you are, even if your name is not well known.
exp.5:8:
This verse says that the king orders that everything needed for worship be given to the priests of Jerusalem: young bulls, rams, and lambs for the burnt offerings (offerings burned up entirely), along with wheat, salt, wine, and oil. It was to be given each day, as the priests requested, "without fail," that is, without placing obstacles or delays in their way.

It is King Darius of Persia who speaks. The enemies of the Jews had halted the rebuilding of the temple, but Darius found the earlier decree of King Cyrus and ordered that the work be supported. The expenses were to come from the taxes collected west of the Euphrates River. The verses that follow say that the king asked them to pray for him and for his sons.

For today: God can move even rulers who do not know him to sustain his work. We can pray for our leaders and, when we serve in the church, be steady and orderly, without neglecting what others need in order to serve.
exp.8:8:
They were slaves, the verse says, yet God did not abandon them. God moved the hearts of the kings of Persia to show compassion and to let them live, rebuild the temple, and raise up its ruins.

Ezra is praying aloud, in sorrow, because some who had returned from exile had mixed with the customs and marriages of the neighboring peoples. Before confessing his sin, he remembers God's goodness. He speaks in the plural, "we," because he identifies himself with the people.

For today: when you fail or find yourself in a bad moment, first remember how God has sustained you. That memory does not lead you to make excuses, but to return to Him with humility and hope.
exp.7:3:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem. It says that from the family of Pahath-moab came a leader named Elihoenai, son of Zerahiah, and with him two hundred males. "Males" refers to adult men, and perhaps also to their families, although the text counts only the men.

Ezra himself is the writer, and he carefully records who returned with him from Babylon, during the reign of Artaxerxes. This list shows that the return was organized and that each group had a recognized leader. Scholars think the name Pahath-moab means something like "governor of Moab," but its exact origin is not entirely clear.

For today: God knows names and not just crowds. Even if your service seems small or little seen, God remembers it. Serve faithfully where you are.
exp.1:0:
This verse opens a list of the families who returned from exile. It says they are "the children of the province," meaning the people of Judah, who went up from Babylon. The exile was a forced removal, and the people who had been taken away by Nebuchadnezzar went back. Each one returned to their own city.

The book of Ezra does not say with certainty who wrote it, although Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra. The narrator tells how God allowed the people to return after about seventy years of exile, following the decree of King Cyrus. This list confirms that these were real people, with names and families, and not a faceless crowd.

For today: God knows each person by name and remembers their place. Even when you sometimes feel lost or far from home, He can bring you back and give you a new beginning.
exp.1:27:
It says 223 men from the towns of Bethel and Ai returned to Judah after the exile in Babylon. The word "men" here simply means men, and it is used to count the people of each town. Bethel means "house of God."

This is part of a long list of families and towns who returned with Zerubbabel and Joshua, when King Cyrus allowed the return. The writer, according to tradition, is Ezra, a priest and scribe. He records the names and figures because each family needed to show its origin in Israel. Some figures in this list differ a little from those in Nehemiah 7, and scholars explain this in several ways, such as different dates of counting or copying errors. There is no single certain answer.

For today: God notices people one by one, even those who seem to be just a number. Your simple and faithful service also counts before Him.
exp.6:9:
This verse says that Ezra had firmly resolved in his heart to do three things: to study the law of God, to put it into practice, and to teach it to Israel. The word "seek" means to investigate and search diligently. The phrase "statutes and judgments" refers to the instructions and just decisions of the law of Moses. The phrase "prepared his heart" speaks of a firm, decided commitment made in advance.

The speaker is the narrator of the book, who explains why the hand of God was upon Ezra on the journey from Babylon to Jerusalem. Ezra was a priest and a scribe, and he was returning with a group of exiles. Many understand that the verse gives the reason for his success: his life was well directed.

For today: before teaching or advising others, seek to know God's Word and to live it yourself first. You can begin with a set time of reading, asking God to help you obey what you learn.
exp.7:16:
Ezra says that he sent a group of leaders with a precise message for Iddo, the leader at a place called Casiphia. Ezra told them exactly what to say.
