The request was for Iddo and his brothers, the temple servants, so that they would bring ministers, that is, men who would serve in the house of God. Ezra sent them and gathered them together, as the verse states.

Ezra speaks here as the one leading a group of Jews back to Jerusalem. When they camped by the river Ahava, he noticed that there were no Levites, those in charge of the service of the temple. Without them, the worship would not have enough servants. Regarding the exact location of Casiphia, there is no certainty.

For today: when something important is missing in the service of God, it is wise to act with order, pray, and ask for help clearly. Ezra did not stay silent or improvise: he planned, communicated clearly what he needed, and trusted in the good hand of God.
exp.5:13:
The verse says that the leaders of the Jews kept on building the temple, and it went well for them. They did this encouraged by what Haggai and Zechariah had prophesied. The phrase "they prospered" means the work moved forward successfully. In the end they finished the work, because God had commanded it and because the Persian kings Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes gave their orders.

The author of the book tells how the second temple in Jerusalem was completed, after the return from exile. The work had stopped because of opposition, and Haggai and Zechariah encouraged the people to take it up again. The Persian kings appear as instruments of God. About Artaxerxes, many scholars note that he reigned after the temple was finished, and there is discussion about why he is mentioned here. Perhaps the reference is to his later support of God's work in Jerusalem.

For today: God often fulfills his purposes by combining his word, our steady effort, and sometimes unexpected authorities. If there is something God has asked of you that has stalled, get moving again with faith, step by step.
exp.7:24:
Here Ezra tells how he weighed out before the priests the silver, the gold and the vessels of the temple. All of this was an offering for the house of God, given by King Artaxerxes, his counselors, his princes and the Israelites who were in Babylon.

Ezra speaks in the first person. He leads a group of Jews returning to Jerusalem and carries these goods with them. Before leaving, they fasted and asked God for protection. Then Ezra chose twelve priests and handed over what had been received, weighing it carefully, so that they would be accountable for it on the journey.

For today: what belongs to God deserves to be handled with honesty and order. If you manage money or responsibilities in your church or family, do so with clarity and transparency, and entrust it to God in prayer.
exp.6:0:
After these events recorded in the earlier chapters, during the reign of Artaxerxes, king of Persia, Ezra appears. He is introduced with his family: he is the son of Seraiah, grandson of Azariah, and great-grandson of Hilkiah. This begins a list of ancestors that continues in the following verses.

Context: the author of the book does not name himself, although Jewish tradition usually attributes it to Ezra himself. It tells the story of the return of the Jews to Jerusalem after the exile. Here the story of Ezra begins. The list of fathers shows that he was a priest, a descendant of Aaron. According to many scholars, this Artaxerxes would be Artaxerxes I, although some propose a different king. Between chapter 6 and chapter 7, about fifty or sixty years pass.

For today: God works through people with history and roots. Give thanks to those who passed on the faith to you, and remember that your service, though it may seem small, is part of God's plan.
exp.3:4:
This verse says that the enemies of the Jews paid money to counselors of the Persian government to ruin the plans of those rebuilding the temple. "Hired counsellors" means people paid to secure favors through money. To frustrate their purpose means to undo or defeat what they had planned. This lasted from the time of Cyrus until the reign of Darius.

The narrator of the book tells what happened after Zerubbabel and Jeshua turned down the help of the neighboring peoples. They felt offended and began to oppose the work. So they used political influence to stop the construction. The text shows that the opposition was not brief, but went on for years.

For today: when you do what is right and meet resistance, do not be surprised or give up quickly. Opposition can be long and deceitful. Remain faithful, act with integrity, and trust that God sustains what he has entrusted to you.
exp.7:25:
It says that Ezra weighed out and handed over to the chosen priests a large amount of silver and gold: about 650 talents of silver, silver vessels worth 100 talents, and 100 talents of gold. A talent was a very large unit of weight. Scholars calculate its weight in different ways, so the modern figures are approximate.

It speaks of Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law. He was returning from Babylon to Jerusalem with a group of exiles. He carried the offerings that the king, his advisers, and the people had given for the temple. For that reason he weighed everything carefully and placed it in the hands of twelve priests, so that they would be accountable for it during the journey.

For today: what belongs to God deserves to be looked after with honesty and order. If you handle money belonging to the church or to others, do it with transparency, with the help of other people, and without carelessness.
exp.4:6:
This verse says that the Persian officials sent a letter to King Darius, and that they opened it with the words "all peace." That was the respectful way to begin an official letter. The sentence about the word "sent" has been removed, since it explained a source-language form.

The speaker here is the narrator of Ezra, who copies the letter from Tatnai, governor of the region west of the river Euphrates, and from his companions. The Jews had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem. The officials wanted to know whether they had permission, so they informed the king. The text says God watched over the Jewish elders, and for that reason the work did not stop while the answer was on its way.

For today: when someone questions or slows down your good work, do not despair. Act with honesty, be patient, and trust that God looks after you even in the middle of other people's paperwork or doubts.
exp.2:7:
It says that, in the second year after arriving in Jerusalem, in the second month, Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the rest of the priests, Levites and those who had come back from the captivity began the work on the temple. They put the Levites from twenty years old and upward in charge of the work. The word "captivity" refers to the exile in Babylon, and "Jerusalem" is the city of Jerusalem.

The text is historical narrative, and it is not certain who wrote the book; tradition connects it with Ezra. The people had returned from exile by the decree of King Cyrus. They were already offering sacrifices, but the temple still needed to be rebuilt. This verse shows the organized start of that work, with clear leadership and a division of responsibilities.

For today: good work moves forward better when each person takes on their part with order and unity. Ask yourself what small responsibility you can take on in your church or family, and begin without waiting for perfect conditions.
exp.1:36:
This verse is part of a list of people. It says that 1,052 descendants of the family of Immer returned to Judea. Immer was one of the priestly families, that is, men devoted to service in the temple. Here "children of" means descendants, not only direct sons.

The book of Ezra records the return of the Jews from Babylon, where they had been exiled, to Jerusalem. The author, traditionally identified with Ezra, carefully notes the families and their numbers. Probably he wanted to show that the people kept their identity and that God was fulfilling his promise to bring them back. The figures in this same record appear with small differences in other texts, and these are explained in several ways.

God knows each person and each family, even when a name seems to be just a detail in a list. Your service, though it may be quiet, has value before him. Today you can be faithful in small things, knowing that God sees them and remembers them.
exp.6:10:
This verse presents the copy of an official letter that King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra. It describes him as a priest and a scribe, that is, an expert in copying, knowing, and teaching the law of God and his commandments for Israel.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who now inserts the king's document. Ezra leaves Babylon with permission from the Persian government. Earlier it was said that the good hand of God was upon him because he had prepared his heart to study the law, keep it, and teach it. Scholars discuss which Artaxerxes this is, but the text shows that God works even through foreign authorities.

For today: before teaching something to others, it is wise to study it with humility and to practice it. Prepare your heart with the Bible, and trust that God can open doors in unexpected ways.
exp.8:6:
This verse says that the people of Israel have lived in serious guilt from the days of their ancestors until today. Because of their sins, both the people and their kings and priests were handed over to foreign kings. They suffered the sword (the blade), exile (captivity), plundering (robbery), and public shame (confusion of face).

Ezra speaks here. He is a priest and teacher of the law. He has just learned that many of those who returned from exile had mixed with the neighboring peoples in practices that go against God's law. Ezra prays on his knees, in grief, and identifies himself with his people, even though he was not the main one to blame.

For today: when we fail, God invites us to acknowledge the truth with humility, without excuses. And like Ezra, we can pray with sincere sorrow, trusting that God remains merciful.
exp.7:29:
This verse says that the priests and the Levites received the silver, the gold, and the vessels, already weighed, to bring them to Jerusalem, to the house of God. The word "weight" reminds us that everything was handed over with exact count.

Ezra, the scribe, is speaking. He leads a group of Jews from Babylon toward Jerusalem. Earlier, he set apart twelve priests and entrusted them with the offerings, which were dedicated to God. Weighing everything before the journey and again on arrival gave openness and protected everyone from suspicion. Afterward, the text says that God delivered them on the road.

For today: when you handle something that belongs to God or to others, such as money, time, or church responsibilities, do it with order, clarity, and honesty. Trusting God does not remove the duty to be careful.
exp.6:27:
This verse says that God caused the king and his counselors to look upon Ezra with kindness. The phrase about God inclining his mercy toward him means that God gave him favor. The king's counselors and his high officials are the people who stood around him in the court, and Ezra's wording for them matches the verse's "counsellors" and "princes." Ezra was encouraged and strengthened, and because of this he gathered the leaders of Israel to return with him to Jerusalem.

Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law, speaks here in the account of his journey from Babylon. He has just quoted the letter of King Artaxerxes, which gave him permission and support to go to Jerusalem. Ezra gives all the credit to God, not to his own ability. When he says "the hand of my God was upon me," he acknowledges that God was guiding and sustaining his mission.

For today: when God opens a door for you or gives you favor, acknowledge it with gratitude. Then be encouraged to act, as Ezra did, who did not simply wait, but gathered others to carry out what God had set in motion.
exp.3:1:
Here some inhabitants of the region approach Zerubbabel and the heads of the families and offer to help rebuild the temple. They say that they too seek the same God and that they have been offering sacrifices to him since the days of Esarhaddon, king of Assyria, who brought them to live there.

The phrase "heads of the families" in this verse refers to the leaders of the households. The Hebrew word "á" is rendered simply as "a" today.

The speakers are the ones called "the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin." They were peoples whom the Assyrian king had settled in the land. Their offer sounded friendly, but the Jewish leaders turned it down, perhaps because their worship was mixed and because King Cyrus had entrusted the work to them. Interpreters differ on the exact motives of these neighbors.

For today: being kind is not enough; it is wise to ask for discernment about the intentions of those who offer to help, without harshness, but with firmness in what God has entrusted to us.
exp.3:10:
This verse presents the copy of an official letter. The word the Bible text uses here means a copy, and the letter is addressed to King Artaxerxes. Those who write it identify themselves as the king's servants from the region beyond the river, that is, officials who lived west of the Euphrates River. The text abbreviates the greeting that would normally follow.

The letter comes from Rehum, Shimshai, and their companions, leaders of peoples who had been settled in the region of Samaria. They opposed the Jews rebuilding Jerusalem. Rather than confronting them directly, they write to the king to present the Jews as a political threat. The verses that follow show that their accusations appealed to the king's fear of losing money and tax revenue.

Today we can learn to be careful with accusations that sound very official or reasonable. Sometimes opposition to what is good is disguised as legitimate concern. Before believing or repeating a complaint, it is wise to ask about the motives of the person making it, and to trust that God cares for his work.
exp.7:19:
This verse says that, besides the Levites, two hundred and twenty Nethinims also joined the journey. The Nethinims were helpers of the temple, that is, people dedicated to serving the Levites in the tasks of worship. The Bible says that David and the princes had appointed them for that service. "All of them were expressed by name" means that each one was written down individually on a list.

Ezra speaks here. He is a priest and teacher of the law. He is gathering a group to return from Babylon to Jerusalem, and he noticed that servants for the temple were missing. So he also gathers these helpers. Shortly after, beside the river Ahava, he proclaims a fast to ask God for protection on the road.

For today: God notices simple service and does not forget anyone. Serve where you can, even when no one applauds you, for your name matters before God.
exp.3:6:
In the days of King Artaxerxes of Persia, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and their other companions sent him a letter. It was written in Syriac, which here means Aramaic, the language used in the administration of the empire, and it was translated into that same language.

The book of Ezra tells how the Jews who returned from exile faced opposition as they rebuilt the temple and the city. Here the author speaks of those who opposed them and sent letters to the king to stop the work. Some scholars think this Artaxerxes is the same one who appears later in the chapter, but there is no full agreement about his exact identity.

For today: opposition sometimes comes with paperwork, accusations, and well-crafted words. Do not be discouraged when your good work is criticized. Keep going with integrity, pray, and trust that God sees what others try to hold back.
exp.4:16:
It says that, if it seems good to the king, the royal archive in Babylon should be searched, where the important documents were kept. They want to confirm whether Cyrus really ordered the house of God to be rebuilt at Jerusalem. They ask the king to send his answer and his decision in writing. The phrase "let the king send his pleasure to us" means "let us know."

The speaker is Tatnai, governor on the other side of the river Euphrates, together with his companions, in a letter to King Darius. The Jews said that Cyrus had given them permission to rebuild, and these officials did not make decisions on their own: they asked to verify the facts. So the work was left waiting for an official answer.

For today: when there are doubts or conflicts, it is wise to seek the truth calmly and in an orderly way, without accusing or acting in haste. And those who work for God can trust that He governs even when everything depends on papers and authorities.
exp.2:6:
The verse tells that the Jews who returned from exile paid money to the carpenters and the stonemasons. They also gave food, drink, and oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre, who were from the cities of Sidon and Tyre. In return, they would bring cedar logs from Lebanon by sea to the port of Joppa.

The writer of the book narrates this, describing how the work of rebuilding the temple was prepared. The sacrifices were already being offered, but the foundations had not yet been laid. It is said that this was in keeping with what Cyrus, king of Persia, had allowed, since he had authorized the return and the work.

For today: serving God is not only worship, it is also planning and working with order. We can pray and, at the same time, prepare with effort what God has entrusted to us.
exp.9:8:
Ezra 10:9 tells us that all the men of Judah and Benjamin came together in Jerusalem within the three days they had been given. It was the twentieth day of the ninth month, roughly December. They sat in the square in front of the temple, trembling because of the matter to be dealt with and also because of the rain. The word "trespassed" in the verse means having seriously failed to do what God commanded.

The one telling the story is Ezra, or someone writing about him. The leaders had summoned everyone who had returned from exile, under the threat of losing their property and being cut off from the community. The problem was that many had married women from neighboring peoples, and the Bible presents this as a threat to the people's faithfulness to God. Some scholars think the trembling showed repentance, while others think it showed fear of the consequences.

Today we can learn to come to God with humility when He points out a mistake. We do not need to wait until the pressure arrives. We should come before Him with sincerity and be willing to change.
exp.9:40:
This verse is part of a list of names: Azareel, Shelemiah, Shemariah. It does not tell a story or give a direct teaching; it simply records specific men. They are among the sons of Bani, according to the context of this list.

The book of Ezra tells of the return of the Jews from exile. In chapter 10, Ezra leads the people to acknowledge that many had married women from neighboring peoples, and this was pulling them away from faithfulness to God. The list names those who took on that commitment. The author, traditionally Ezra, wanted to keep a record with real names. Scholars discuss how to understand this decision, but the text shows the people's desire to return to God.

God knows each person by name; none of them is a mere number. It also reminds us that turning back and correcting our course is something concrete, done through real decisions and with an open face. Today we can ask ourselves: what concrete step is God asking of me to return to Him?
exp.7:7:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned to Jerusalem. It says that from the descendants of Shephatiah, a man named Zebadiah, son of Michael, led the group, and that with him were eighty males. The word "males" refers to adult men, probably heads of families or leaders.

The writer is Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law, who narrates in the first person the departure from Babylon toward Jerusalem under King Artaxerxes. He carefully records the name of each leader and the number of those who went with him. Scholars agree that this list shows the return was orderly and that each family was important to God's people.

For today: God knows each person by name, even when a name seems to be just one more entry in a list. Your service, though simple or little seen, counts before Him. Today, offer to help in your church or family without seeking recognition.
exp.1:63:
This verse says that the whole people who returned from exile in Babylon, counted as one community, came to 42,360 people. The phrase "united as one man" means they were counted as one body, all together. "Congregation" means assembly or gathered people.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, traditionally thought to be Ezra. After Cyrus's decree, these families returned to Judah with Zerubbabel. The list shows that God preserved his people and that each family mattered. The verse before it speaks of priests without a genealogical record, who were set apart for a time. In this way the holiness of service to God was guarded. The figures in the lists of Ezra and Nehemiah differ slightly, and scholars explain this in several ways.

For today: God knows and counts his people. No one is a mere number to him. Serve your church with the confidence that your place matters.
exp.4:12:
This verse says that in the first year of Cyrus as king of Babylon, Cyrus himself issued an order for the house of God in Jerusalem to be rebuilt. The word "but" that opens the verse introduces a contrast with what came before, and the phrase "made a decree" means that he gave an official order.

Here the Jewish leaders, Zerubbabel and Jeshua, according to the book, answer Tattenai, a Persian governor, who asked them by what authority they were building. They explain that the temple was destroyed because of the sin of the people, but that they now have a royal authorization. They appeal to a decree of Cyrus, who had conquered Babylon.

For today: when we do something good and someone questions us, we can respond with humility, honesty, and trust that God works even through authorities who do not know him. He fulfills his purposes in his time.
exp.8:12:
This verse says that although the people have suffered greatly for their wicked deeds and their great guilt, God did not punish them as much as they deserved. The phrase about God holding back the full punishment means that God stopped the complete judgment from falling on them. The word for the group that survived refers to the remnant that was left alive and was able to return to their land.

Ezra speaks in prayer to God. He has just learned that many Israelites who returned from exile had married people from neighboring nations who practiced things God rejected. Ezra does not make excuses: he acknowledges the guilt and is amazed at the mercy of God.

For today: when we fail, let us neither downplay the wrong nor sink into despair. Let us honestly acknowledge what we did, thank God that He gives us another chance, and use that grace to change, not to repeat the same thing.
exp.3:0:
This verse says that the enemies of Judah and Benjamin learned that those who had returned from exile in Babylon were rebuilding the temple of the LORD, the God of Israel. The words "when they heard" or "on learning" express how they came to know this. The word "captivity" refers to the time when the people were taken captive to Babylon.

The narrator of the book goes on to tell what happened after the return, when Zerubbabel and others began to raise up the temple. These "adversaries" were people who lived in the region, brought there by the Assyrians. They seemed friendly, but their intentions were not clear. What follows shows that the leaders of Israel turned down their offer of help.

Today, when we do something for God, not everyone who offers to help is seeking the same thing we are. Let us ask for wisdom to discern, and be firm yet kind in what God has entrusted to us.
exp.1:67:
This verse tells that some of the heads of the families, upon arriving at the place in Jerusalem where the temple had stood, gave offerings of their own free will. They wanted to help rebuild the house of God on the same site where it had stood before.

The reader will see the word "chief" in the verse, so the verse's comment on the phrase "heads of the fathers" can be rewritten: "chief" refers to the leaders of each family or clan.

No one speaks directly here; this is the writer's account, which lists those who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. After listing people and animals, he highlights that some of the leaders gave beyond what was expected. The following verses say they gave according to their ability, that is, in line with what they could afford.

For today: God values generosity that comes from the heart, not giving done out of obligation. Think about what you can give to your church or community, whether time, talent, or money, according to your means, and do it with joy.
exp.2:11:
This verse tells how, when the foundations of the new temple were laid, some of the older men wept loudly and others shouted aloud for joy. The older men were priests, Levites, and heads of families who had seen the first temple. The heads of the families are the leaders of the households.

The narrator is the writer of Ezra, who tells what happened when the people returned from exile in Babylon. The people had just begun rebuilding the temple and celebrated with trumpets, cymbals, and songs. The older men remembered Solomon's temple, which was greater. The text does not explain why they wept; it could be sadness, longing, or emotion, and perhaps all of these together.

For today: God can receive our tears and our joy at the same time. We can remember with pain what was lost and still celebrate the new thing He begins, without despising small beginnings.
exp.5:20:
This verse says that the Israelites who had returned from exile ate the Passover. Others also ate it, people who had separated themselves from the defiling practices of the peoples of the land. The exile in Babylon is what is meant by the return from captivity, and the defiling practices were ones that did not please God. All of them were united by one purpose: to seek the Lord, the God of Israel.

The book of Ezra recounts the people's return to Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the temple. Here the narrator tells us that the temple was already finished and that they celebrated the Passover. Those who joined them were probably people living in the land who decided to leave behind their former practices. The details of exactly who they were are not explained.

For today: seeking God means leaving behind what pulls us away from Him. The door is open to anyone who wants to draw near with sincerity, regardless of their past.
exp.1:39:
This verse lists the Levites who returned from exile in Babylon. They belonged to the families of Jeshua, Kadmiel, and Hodaviah, and in total they numbered seventy-four people. The Levites were the tribe responsible for serving in the temple and helping the priests.

Ezra here copies an official list of those who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel, after about seventy years of exile. The speaker is the narrator, and his purpose is to record the families who rebuilt the life of the people. What stands out is that the Levites were few, only seventy-four, compared with the priests, who were more than four thousand. The texts do not explain the reason with certainty.

God takes into account each person who serves him, even when that service is small and almost no one notices it. Your faithful service, though it may seem small, has value before him.
exp.9:17:
This verse begins the list of the priests who had married foreign women. First come the descendants of Jeshua, son of Jozadak, and his brothers: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah. "Were found" means that their case was confirmed after an investigation.

The one telling the story is Ezra, or an account that follows his perspective. After the return from exile, the people had mixed their lives with the religious customs of the neighboring nations. A commission reviewed the cases one by one over about three months. That families of priests appear, including the family of the high priest of that time, shows that the failure reached the leaders. How to understand and apply this harsh measure today is something that is debated.

For today: honesty begins with those who lead. Ask God to show you the areas where you need to correct your course, without excuses or comparisons.
exp.3:14:
This verse is part of a letter of accusation. The authors ask the king to search the "book of the histories," that is, the official records of the earlier kings. They say that there he will find that Jerusalem was a rebellious city, harmful to kings and provinces, and that for a long time revolts were stirred up there. For that reason, they claim, it was destroyed. "Harmful" means hurtful, and "stirred up revolts" means that they organized uprisings.

The speakers are Rehum, Simsai, and their companions, officials who lived in Samaria and its surroundings. They write to the Persian king to stop the rebuilding of Jerusalem. They present themselves as loyal to the king, but they also look after their own interests. They use part of the history to frighten the king and achieve their goal.

Today we can learn not to be carried away by half-truths. Before believing an accusation, it is wise to listen calmly and seek the complete facts.
exp.3:19:
It says that in Jerusalem there were powerful kings who ruled over the whole region beyond the Euphrates River, and that the people paid them taxes. "They ruled" means they held dominion or governed. The phrase "toll, tribute, and custom" refers to different kinds of compulsory payments: tribute is what subject peoples paid, a head tax was a personal levy, and custom was what was charged for the use of roads or land.

The speaker is the Persian king Artaxerxes, responding to a letter from his officials against the Jews who were rebuilding Jerusalem. After reviewing the records, he confirms that the city once had strong kings, such as David and Solomon. He uses this to justify halting the work, out of fear that the city might rebel again. It is a decision based on history and political fear.

For today: before judging someone by their past, it is wise to look at who they are now. An old record does not always tell the whole truth about the present.
exp.5:9:
This verse says that the Jews are to offer acceptable sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and of his sons. The phrase "sweet savours" in the King James Version refers to offerings with a pleasing aroma, which please God. Some translators render it as "acceptable sacrifices."

The one speaking is King Darius of Persia. The enemies of the Jews had halted the rebuilding of the temple, but Darius searched out the earlier decree of King Cyrus and confirmed it. He ordered the costs of the temple to be paid from the royal revenues and asked for prayers for his family. The text does not fully explain why he asked for this.

For today: Paul encourages prayer for those who govern (1 Timothy 2:1-2). Pray this week for your leaders, even if you do not think as they do, asking for wisdom and justice for them.
exp.4:7:
He says that Tatnai and his companions went to the land of Judea and saw the temple of God, which they describe as "the great God." They describe it as built with great stones (probably large stones, perhaps white or carved), with timber laid in the walls. They say the work goes on fast, that is, quickly, and that it prospers in their hands, that is, it is going well for them.

The one speaking is Tatnai, a Persian governor west of the Euphrates River. He writes an official report to King Darius after inspecting the work. He does so because the Jews were rebuilding the temple and he wanted to know whether they had permission. His tone is neutral, but he acknowledges that the work is going well.

For today: when you do what God has entrusted to you, your steadfastness can be a witness, even to those who do not believe. Keep working faithfully, even when you are questioned; God can make your effort prosper.
exp.1:33:
It says that 345 descendants of families who lived in Jericho returned from exile in Babylon to the land of Judah. It is part of a list of families, cities, and groups that came back. "Children of" means descendants or members of that family or place.

The book of Ezra records this list after King Cyrus allowed the Jews to return. Jewish tradition attributes the book to Ezra, though not everyone agrees on how it was put together. The list is written to show that God kept his promise to restore his people and that every family mattered. The numbers in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 have small differences, and scholars explain them in various ways.

For today: God does not see his people as a faceless crowd. Your name and your service, though they may seem small, matter to him. Today you can value and encourage someone who works quietly in your church or family.
exp.6:4:
This verse continues the list of Ezra's ancestors. It says he descended from Abishua, from Phinehas, from Eleazar, and from Aaron, "the chief priest." That is, Ezra belonged to the priestly family that began with Aaron, the brother of Moses. The name spelled "Phinehas" here, and "chief priest" means the first high priest of Israel.

The book of Ezra introduces its main character here, before telling the story of his journey from Babylon to Jerusalem. The author, whom tradition usually identifies with Ezra himself (though not all agree), wants to show that Ezra had the right to teach and to serve. Some scholars think the list leaves out some names, which is common in biblical genealogies.

For today: God works through generations. What we receive from our family or our faith is a legacy, but also a responsibility. Ask yourself what you can pass on today, faithfully and steadily, to those who come after you.
exp.7:20:
Ezra tells us that, beside the river Ahava, he proclaimed a fast. "Afflict ourselves" meant humbling themselves before God, acknowledging that they needed him. They asked for a "right way," that is, a safe journey without stumbling, for themselves, their little ones, and all their substance.

Ezra was a priest and a teacher of the law, leading a group of Jews from Babylon toward Jerusalem. The road was long and dangerous. He had told the king that God watches over those who seek him, so he was ashamed to ask for soldiers. He preferred to trust God and asked for his help through fasting.

For today: before a journey, a move, or an important decision, we can pause to pray with humility, placing our families and our belongings in God's hands. This does not remove our responsibility to be prudent, but it reminds us that our final trust is in him.
exp.1:69:
After returning from exile in Babylon, each group settled in its own cities: the priests, the Levites (assistants at the temple), part of the people, the singers, the porters (guards of the temple gates), and the Nethinims (servants dedicated to the work of the temple). In the end, all Israel was living in their cities.

It is part of the account in the book of Ezra, which describes the return of the Jews to their land. It is not known for certain who wrote the book; tradition names Ezra. This verse closes the list of those who came back and of the freewill offerings to rebuild the temple. It shows that the people reorganized themselves in an orderly way, each in their place and with their service.

For today: God values every kind of service, from the one who sings to the one who guards the gate. Ask yourself what your place is, and do it with generosity and faithfulness.
exp.4:14:
King Cyrus, according to this passage, handed over to Sheshbazzar the vessels of the temple and ordered him to carry them to Jerusalem, place them in the temple, and rebuild the house of God in its former place, that is, where it stood before.

Jerusalem is the city named in the verse, and the vessels are the sacred objects used in worship.

The speakers here are the Jewish leaders of Jerusalem, who are answering Tatnai, the Persian governor. He had asked them by what authority they were building. They cite what Cyrus commanded years earlier and ask that the royal archive in Babylon be searched to confirm it. Scholars often identify Sheshbazzar as a Jewish leader with an official position, and some connect him with Zerubbabel, though that is debated.

God can fulfill his purposes even through rulers who do not know him. If your own project today seems stalled or questioned, keep going with patience and honesty, trust that God knows how to restore what was lost, and do not be afraid to seek clarity.
exp.1:24:
This verse says that 743 descendants of three towns, Kirjath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, returned from exile in Babylon. "The children of" here does not mean only children, but families or descendants of those places. Ancient place names are spelled differently today: Chîriath-jearim is the same as Kirjath-jearim.

Ezra does not speak in the first person; it is the account of the writer, who lists those who returned to Judea with Zerubbabel after the decree of King Cyrus. The list, which is repeated with small differences in Nehemiah 7, shows that the people returned by families and cities. Scholars explain the differences in some figures in several ways, and there is no single certain answer.

For today: God pays attention to specific people, even when they seem to be only a number. Your service, though it may be quiet, counts for Him and is part of something greater.
exp.1:53:
This verse mentions only two families: the descendants of Neziah and those of Hatipha. "Children of" does not refer only to direct sons and daughters, but to a whole family or clan descended from an ancestor with that name.

It is part of the list of Jews who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. Ezra, the scribe to whom the book is traditionally attributed, records the names with care. These two families appear among the temple servants. Beyond their names, we know nothing more about Neziah and Hatipha.

God notices people whom the world would overlook. These families did nothing famous, yet they were written down. Today you can serve faithfully in simple tasks, without applause, trusting that God sees and values your work.
exp.8:11:
The passage says the people must not give their daughters in marriage to the sons of the neighboring peoples, nor take their daughters for their own sons, nor seek their friendship or their prosperity. "Strengthened" means made strong, "inheritance" is the land passed down to heirs, and "seek their friendship" means looking for their goodwill or a binding agreement. The goal was that Israel would live strong, enjoy the good fruits of the land, and leave it to their children.

Ezra speaks in prayer to God. They have returned from exile in Babylon and discover that many had married women from peoples with idolatrous practices. Ezra cites a warning from the prophets and mourns, fearing that God will be angry once again. The texts of the Law tie this prohibition to the danger of idolatry. Some scholars stress the religious side more than the ethnic one.

Today we can make sure that our most important decisions, such as dating, business partners, or close friendships, do not draw us away from God. We can love everyone, but ask God for wisdom so that we do not give way on what sustains our faith.
exp.2:10:
When the foundation of the new temple was laid, the people sang and gave thanks to the Lord. Here "confessing" means acknowledging and proclaiming who God is. They repeated: "He is good, and his mercy (his faithful love) endures forever toward Israel." All the people shouted with great joy, because the foundation of God's house was being laid.

This happened when the Jews returned from exile in Babylon and began rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem. The priests with trumpets and the Levites with cymbals praised according to the order left by King David. The people speak because God allowed them to return and begin again.

For today: do not wait until everything is finished before giving thanks. Even in the small beginnings of something God has placed in your hands, you can praise him for his goodness and his faithfulness.
exp.8:1:
They say that the Israelites married their sons to women from the neighboring peoples, and gave their daughters to men of those peoples. Thus "the holy seed," that is, the people set apart for God, mixed itself with them. Breaking faith means betraying or seriously failing a commitment. Most serious of all: the leaders set the bad example.

The leaders of the people report to Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law, after the return from exile in Babylon. The problem was not race, but that these marriages led them to imitate idolatrous practices, as the law of Moses warned. Ezra reacts with grief and astonishment, tearing his clothing.

For today: Those who have influence, in the family, the church, or at work, teach more by their example than by their words. Ask God to help you be faithful in what others see, and weep sincerely when you realize you have drifted away from Him.
exp.1:68:
This verse tells how the Israelites, each according to their means, gave to the one in charge of the money a great offering for the work of the temple: gold coins, silver, and one hundred garments for the priests. "Drams" were coins or weights of gold, and "pounds" were units of weight for the silver. Scholars are not sure of their exact equivalent today.

The account is written by a narrator who, according to tradition, was Ezra. It speaks of the Jews who returned from exile in Babylon. Some heads of families offered willingly to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem. The offering is recorded to remember that the temple was raised with the participation of the people.

For today: give joyfully and according to your means. God looks not only at the amount, but at a heart willing to serve him and to support his work.
exp.7:32:
It says that on the fourth day after arriving in Jerusalem, the silver, the gold and the vessels of the temple were weighed in the house of God. Four men did this: Meremoth the priest, with Eleazar, and the Levites Jozabad and Noadiah.

The phrase "was weighed then" means it was weighed right away, and the word "vessels" refers to the utensils used in worship. [Note: this sentence is removed per instructions.]

Ezra speaks, recounting the journey from Babylon. Along the way God had protected them from enemies and ambushes. Now they hand over the offerings they had brought for the temple. Everything was counted and weighed, and the weight was recorded, so that nothing would be lost and no one could suspect them.

For today: handle with order and transparency what others entrust to us, whether money, time or responsibilities. Honesty does not get in the way of faith; it is a way of honoring God and caring for the trust of others.
exp.2:3:
This verse tells us that the people kept the Feast of Booths, also called the Feast of Tabernacles or of Shelters, as the Scripture commands. In addition, they offered burnt offerings (sacrifices that were burned whole on the altar) every day. They did this by number, that is, in the set amount, and according to the custom, with each offering on its own day.

The book of Ezra tells of the return of the Jews from exile in Babylon. The writer, who narrates the account, describes how Jeshua the priest and Zerubbabel the leader first rebuilt the altar, even though they were afraid of the neighboring peoples. They had not yet laid the foundations of the temple, but they wanted to begin by worshiping God and obeying his law.

For today: do not wait until everything is in order to return to God. Even amid fears and unfinished things, you can begin with a simple and steady obedience, such as praying and giving thanks each day.
exp.8:13:
It would be folly to again break God's commandments and marry into peoples who practice things God abhors. "Breaking" the commandments means violating them, and "joining in marriage" means becoming related by marriage. "Being angry with great harshness" means becoming very fiercely angry. Ezra asks whether God would not be so angry that He would destroy them, leaving no survivors and no way of escape.

Ezra speaks in prayer, after learning that many Israelites, including leaders, had mixed themselves with the neighboring peoples. That mixing put them at risk of following their idolatrous practices. Ezra remembers that God had already treated them with mercy, leaving a remnant that returned from exile, and it shames him that they would fail again.

For today: when God gives us a new opportunity, we should not take it lightly. If something draws us away from Him, the best thing is to acknowledge it with humility, ask for forgiveness, and change direction, giving thanks for His mercy.
exp.1:41:
This verse says that among those who returned from exile in Babylon there was a family of gatekeepers, that is, those in charge of guarding the doors of the temple. Six family groups are named: Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita and Shobai. Together they added up to one hundred thirty-nine people.

This is part of a long list of those who went back to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. The text has no speaker in the foreground; it is a record that the author, traditionally associated with Ezra, preserves. The list showed who belonged to the people and to each service, and it helped to reorganize life in the temple. The gatekeepers appear after the Levites and the singers, and they were far more numerous than them.

For today: God notices simple, little-seen work. Although guarding a door may seem like a small thing, it was written down with names and numbers. Serve faithfully where you are, even when no one notices.
exp.6:15:
This verse says that Ezra could gather all the silver and gold he could find in the province of Babylon. He would also receive the freewill offerings of the people and the priests, given willingly for the house of God in Jerusalem.

The speaker is the Persian king Artaxerxes, in an official letter addressed to Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law. The king gives him permission to travel to Jerusalem with any Jews who wished to go. He charges Ezra with carrying these gifts for worship in the temple. It is remarkable that a foreign king would support the worship of the God of Israel. The Bible presents this as part of God's work on behalf of his people.

God takes pleasure in what we give freely and joyfully, not out of obligation. We might ask ourselves: what can I offer God today with a willing heart, whether time, money, or service?
exp.1:56:
This verse continues the list of families of Solomon's servants who returned to Judea after the exile in Babylon. Four more groups are named here: the children of Shephatiah, of Hattil, of Pochereth of Zebaim, and of Ami. The ancient names sound unusual, but they are the family names of ancestral households. At the end, everything is added up: 392 people among these servants and the Nethinim, who were helpers of the temple.

The book of Ezra preserves an official record, probably written by Ezra or taken from archives of that time. It noted who returned with Zerubbabel to rebuild the temple. Each name mattered for ordering the life of the people.

For today: God does not see anyone as a faceless number. Even those who did simple work were written into his story. Serve him faithfully in the small things; your quiet work also counts before him.
exp.9:0:
Ezra 10:1 tells us that Ezra was praying and confessing the sin of the people. He was weeping and lying face down on the ground before the temple. Then a very large crowd of men, women, and children gathered around him, and everyone was crying with great sorrow.

Ezra was a priest and a teacher of the law. He had learned that many Israelites, including some leaders, had married women from neighboring peoples who worshiped other gods. This put the people's faithfulness to God at risk. Ezra does not accuse harshly; he grieves and prays as if the sin were his own too. That grief moves the people to repent. The measures that follow are difficult, and they should be read carefully within their historical context.

For today: when we see failings around us, let us begin with humility and sincere prayer, not with criticism. A broken heart can encourage others to return to God.
exp.2:4:
This verse says that, after the Feast of Tabernacles, the people kept offering their sacrifices to God on the altar. There was the continual burnt offering (the one burned completely each day), the offerings for the new moons (the beginning of each month), and the offerings for all the feasts set apart for the Lord. There were also voluntary offerings and freewill gifts, that is, those that someone gave on their own initiative, without being commanded to do so.

The text is narrated by the author of the book, who tells how the Jews returned from exile in Babylon. With Jeshua and Zerubbabel as leaders, they rebuilt the altar even though they were afraid of the neighboring peoples. They wanted to restore worship according to the law of Moses, even before they had the temple.

For today: rather than waiting for perfect conditions, we can put God first with steadiness. A daily prayer and an offering given cheerfully can sustain our faith, even in times of fear.
exp.3:8:
This verse begins to name those who signed a letter of accusation. Rehum was the chancellor, something like a high government official, and Shimshai was the scribe, the one who drafted the documents. Together with them were their companions, people from several peoples who lived in the region. The words "chancellor" and "scribe" are official titles, and the names of the peoples are ancient; not all of them can be identified with certainty.

The Jews who had returned from exile were rebuilding the temple and the walls of Jerusalem. Their neighbors in the region opposed them and wrote to the Persian king Artaxerxes to halt the work. This group spoke on behalf of many peoples who had been relocated to Samaria.

Today, opposition to what is good sometimes comes with signatures and documents that look very official. If God has called you to a task, do not be discouraged by criticism; keep going with patience and trust that he sustains his work.
exp.9:4:
Ezra stood up and made the chief priests, the Levites, and all Israel swear a solemn oath that they would carry out what Shecaniah had just proposed. They swore that they would do it. The word "sware" means that they made the promise in the presence of God.

Ezra was praying and weeping over the sin of the people: many who had returned from exile had married women from neighboring nations, and this was pulling them away from God and his law. Shecaniah proposed making a covenant to send away those women and their children. This is a difficult passage, and many readers understand it in different ways. The focus of the text is the fear of falling into idolatry.

For today: when we recognize that something is pulling us away from God, lamenting is not enough. Concrete decisions are needed, taken with humility, and we should seek the support of trusted brothers and sisters in order to remain faithful.
exp.8:9:
Here Ezra says, in prayer, that he has no excuse before God. After receiving so much mercy, the people turned back to disobedience. "Forsaken thy commandments" means that they turned away from what God had commanded them. The question "what shall we say?" shows shame: there is no possible defense.

Ezra speaks on behalf of the people who returned from exile in Babylon. God had given them a remnant and a secure place (a stake) in his sanctuary. But Ezra learns that many, even leaders, had married people from the neighboring nations who practiced customs God had forbidden. So he confesses the sin with grief.

For today: when we fail, there is no need to invent excuses. We can remember how much goodness we have received from God and return to him with sincerity, asking for forgiveness and help to obey him again.
exp.9:6:
This verse says that a public notice was sent throughout Judah and Jerusalem. All who had returned from exile, the ones who had been carried away to Babylon and then came back, were to gather in Jerusalem.

Ezra had been deeply grieved because some of the people, including leaders, had married women from other nations, and this was pulling them away from faithfulness to God. After praying and fasting, Ezra got the people to commit to correcting the problem. Now everyone is called together to deal with the matter as one.

For today: when a mistake affects the whole community, it is not wise to cover it up or fix it in secret. It is good to come together with humility, listen to God, and decide together to return to his way.
exp.5:21:
The returning exiles of Israel kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with joy. God gave them that joy and turned the heart of the king so that he supported them. In this way he gave them strength to finish the work on the temple.

The account is told by the author of the book, traditionally identified as Ezra. He has just described the dedication of the temple and the Passover. The Persian king is called the king of Assyria, probably because he ruled over those ancient lands. This is recorded to show that God cared for his people and moved the rulers to favor his work.

For today: when a difficult task comes through, do not credit it only to your own effort. Give thanks to God, who can give encouragement, open doors, and change hearts. Celebrating with gratitude reminds us that he is the one who sustains our work.
exp.3:18:
The king says that he gave an order to investigate, and in the records they found that Jerusalem, for a long time, has risen up against kings, has rebelled, and has stirred up uprisings. "Uprising" means a rising up or revolt against authority. "Commanded" here means that he gave the order to carry out the search.

The speaker is the Persian king Artaxerxes, responding to a letter from Rehum and Shimshai, who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem. They had accused the city of being rebellious. The king relied on royal records, but he listened only to the accusers, and for that reason he halted the work.

Today we can learn not to judge anyone solely by their past or by what others say. Before condemning, let us listen with justice. And if we are accused unjustly, let us keep trusting in God.
exp.2:5:
They began offering burnt offerings to God from the first day of the seventh month, even though the foundation of the temple had not yet been laid. A burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned completely on the altar.

The author of the book, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain, tells what happened when the Jews returned from exile in Babylon. Under Zerubbabel and the priest Jeshua, they first rebuilt the altar and resumed worship according to the law of Moses. The worship did not wait for the building to be ready. The first thing was to put God back at the center.

For today: do not wait until everything is perfect to worship God. Even if your life, your church, or your plans are still under construction, you can begin today with prayer, gratitude, and obedience. God looks at the heart that is given to Him.
exp.6:19:
If Ezra needed anything more for the temple of God in Jerusalem, and what had already been handed over was not enough, he could take it from the storehouses where the king kept his riches.

The speaker is the Persian king Artaxerxes, in an official letter addressed to Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law. He sends him to Jerusalem with permission and financial support for the worship of God. Scholars agree that this was a political and religious decision of the king, although the Bible shows that God was at work in the heart of that ruler (Ezra 7:27).

For today: when God gives you a task, he often also opens the way to sustain it. Do faithfully what is yours to do, ask with confidence for what is needed, and give thanks for help that arrives, even by unexpected means.
exp.4:2:
This verse tells how a governor named Tatnai, who was in charge of the region west of the Euphrates River, came with Shethar-boznai and their companions. They asked the Jews who had given them permission to rebuild the temple and raise its walls again. Here "governor" is the word for the one in charge, and "raise its walls again" means to build them back up.

The speaker is Tatnai, an official of the Persian empire. The Jews had returned from exile and resumed the work on the temple, encouraged by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah. Tatnai was carrying out an official inspection. The passage shows that God watched over his people: the work did not stop while the matter was being investigated.

For today: when someone questions you for doing what God has asked of you, do not lose heart. Answer with respect, clarity and humility, and keep going, trusting that God cares for you and for his work.
exp.1:58:
These people were part of a group who returned from exile in Babylon, coming from places called Tel-melah, Tel-harsa, Cherub, Addan, and Immer. They could not prove with documents or records that their families belonged to Israel. "Lineage" means the line of ancestors of a family.

The book of Ezra lists those who returned to Judah after the exile. The author, traditionally identified with Ezra, kept careful records because family and tribal identity mattered for the land and for service in the temple. Nothing indicates that they were false Israelites; they simply lacked written proof. The verses that follow show that this had consequences, especially for some priests.

For today: our identity before God does not depend on papers or a family tree, but on his grace. Even so, let us value being sincere and orderly people, and let us welcome with kindness those who feel they have no clear place among God's people.
exp.9:39:
This verse says that Machnadebai, Shashai and Sharai are in a list of men. They were Israelites who, after the return from exile in Babylon, had taken foreign wives. In the version your reader sees, the names are spelled somewhat differently from how we see them today.

Ezra 10 is the end of the book. The writer, traditionally Ezra, records in detail who had done this, after the people repented and committed themselves to correct it. The concern was that they would turn away from God, as had happened before with their ancestors. Scholars understand in different ways how each case was handled, but the text shows that no one was left hidden.

For today: God knows each person by name, even when they fail. If something in your life is pulling you away from Him, do not hide it. Acknowledge it honestly, ask for forgiveness, and take concrete steps to return to Him.
exp.5:16:
It says that at the dedication of the rebuilt temple, the people offered many animals as sacrifices: one hundred bulls, two hundred rams, and four hundred lambs. Also, they offered twelve male goats (the male goats of the flock) to cover the sin of the people. There were twelve, one for each tribe of Israel.

It is part of the account in the book of Ezra, written in the third person. The Jews who returned from exile in Babylon finished the temple under the Persian king Darius, after years of opposition. The twelve male goats show that they saw themselves as one people of twelve tribes, even though they were few and came mostly from Judah. Scholars understand this as a sign of unity and of hope.

Before celebrating, they acknowledged their need for forgiveness. Today we can do the same: when God gives us a victory or completes a work in our life, let us give thanks to him with joy, but also with humility, remembering that everything depends on his forgiveness.
exp.3:7:
This verse tells us that Rehum, who was the chancellor (a kind of governor or head of an office), and Shimshai, the scribe (the one who wrote out documents), wrote a letter against Jerusalem to King Artaxerxes. The words "in this sort" mean that what follows is the text of that letter.

The book of Ezra tells how the Jews who had returned from exile wanted to rebuild the temple and the city. Their neighbors in the region, who were not part of the Jewish people, opposed them. Since they could not stop them by force, they used letters and accusations before the Persian authorities. Scholars debate exactly which king this Artaxerxes was, and the text changes here from Hebrew to Aramaic.

For today: opposition sometimes comes with words and accusations, not with blows. When you do what is right and are criticized, keep going calmly and trust that God sees everything.
exp.6:23:
This verse says that no one could collect taxes from those who served in the temple. "Tribute" was a payment to the government, a "poll tax" was a personal tax, and "rent" was a payment for the use of land or for goods. The "Nethinims" were assistants of the temple, and the "porters" took care of the gates.

The one speaking is the Persian king Artaxerxes, in a letter he gives to Ezra. He wanted to support worship in Jerusalem and not provoke the anger of the God of heaven. Historians debate some details of the date, but the text shows that God moved the heart of a foreign king.

For today: God can use those in authority to care for those who serve him. Pray for your rulers, and give generously to those who serve in your church.
exp.5:3:
This verse describes how the temple was to be built: with three rows of great stones and a row of new timber. "Rows" means the layers or courses of the wall. Also, the cost of the work would be paid from the king's treasury.

Some scholars think the word for "great stones" may refer to large, heavy stones that were not polished. The original term is uncertain.

Here an official document is quoted, found in the archives of Media. It contains the decree of King Cyrus. Neighboring governors had halted the work on the temple, and King Darius ordered this record to be searched. In this way it was confirmed that the rebuilding had royal permission and financial support.

For today: God can watch over his work using unexpected means and people. When you face opposition for doing what is right, trust that he knows how to open paths, and move forward with patience, order, and gratitude.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that the descendants of the family of Bezai who returned were 323 people. "Children of" means descendants, not only direct sons. "Three hundred twenty and three" is the same as three hundred and twenty-three.

The author of the book, whom tradition identifies with Ezra, records the list of the Jews who returned to Jerusalem after the exile in Babylon. He wanted to keep a record of who they were, family by family, to acknowledge their heritage and their place among God's people. In Nehemiah 7:23 Bezai appears with 324, and the reason for the difference is not known for certain. Some think of different records or ways of counting.

Today it reminds us that God knows each person and each family, even those who seem small. Value your place in the community of faith and serve faithfully, even when few notice your name.
exp.1:38:
This verse says that the descendants of Harim who returned from exile numbered 1,017 people. "Children of" means descendants of a family or clan. Harim, Immer, and Pashur were families of priests, so this part of the list counts the priests who returned.

Ezra 2 is a record of the people who returned to Judah from Babylon, after decades of exile, when King Cyrus allowed the rebuilding of the temple. The author, traditionally Ezra, carefully noted the numbers of each family. In this way the identity of the people was preserved and it was confirmed who could serve as priests. The list in Nehemiah 7 is similar, though with some differences in certain figures, and the reason is not known with certainty.

For today: God values every person and every family, even when their name seems to be just a piece of data. Your service, even the kind that goes unnoticed, matters to his work. Take part faithfully in your church, knowing that God knows you.
exp.1:46:
The text says that the descendants of three families, Giddel, Gahar, and Reaiah, returned from exile in Babylon. They belong to a group called "temple servants," who helped the priests and Levites in the service of the temple. "Children of" means families or descendants, not only direct sons.

The passage is a list of the people who returned to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel. It is an official record, probably written by Ezra or compiled from documents of that time. Its purpose was to show who belonged to God's people and had the right to serve in the restored land. Some names vary a little in Nehemiah 7, and it is not known with certainty why.

For today: God remembers even the names almost no one knows. If your work in the church goes unnoticed, take heart: God sees your faithful service and values it. Serve with joy, even when no one applauds you.
exp.9:32:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that seven men from the family of Hashum (Mattenai, Mattathah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei) had taken foreign wives. In some older editions certain names are spelled differently than we see them today, but they are real people in the community.

Ezra 10 tells how, after returning from exile in Babylon, some Israelites married women from neighboring peoples who worshiped other gods. The passage is not a speech but a written record. The leaders noted each man by family, and the people acknowledged their wrong and decided to correct it. How this was carried out is a difficult question, and readers have understood it in various ways.

For today: God notices each person, by name and family. Just as here no one was left anonymous, we too are accountable for our decisions. Let us ask God for sincerity to recognize where we have turned away from him, and for humility to return.
exp.1:44:
This verse continues a list of families called "Nethinim." It mentions three of them: the children of Lebanah, of Hagabah, and of Akkub. They were descended from people who served in the temple, helping the Levites with humble tasks. The word "children" here means descendants or family, not only direct sons and daughters.

The book of Ezra is a historical record, and no narrator speaks directly in this list. It records the Jews who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem after the decree of Cyrus. The names were noted to confirm who belonged to the people and to which service they were assigned. Not much is known with certainty about the meanings of these names.

God remembers even those who did work that was rarely seen. Their names were written down. Today, if you serve quietly in your church or community, your labor does not go unnoticed by God. Serve him with joy, without seeking applause.
exp.0:8:
This verse begins the list of the temple objects that Cyrus returned. It mentions thirty gold bowls, a thousand silver ones, and twenty-nine knives. The words for "bowls" and "knives" are translated in different ways, because the exact meaning of the Hebrew is not entirely certain. The word for "number" here means an inventory or an accounting.

The account, which tradition attributes to Ezra though this is not certain, says that Nebuchadnezzar carried these objects away from Jerusalem. Now Cyrus, king of Persia, returns them through his treasurer, and Sheshbazzar, prince of Judah, receives them. The author gives exact figures to show that everything was handed over in good order. The numbers in the list do not add up to the total of 5,400, and scholars explain this in several ways.

For today: God cares about details and faithfulness in small things. We can honestly look after what is entrusted to us, whether money, time, or service in the church.
exp.0:6:
This verse tells how King Cyrus of Persia ordered the sacred objects of the temple in Jerusalem to be brought out. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had taken them years earlier and placed them in the temple of his gods. The "vessels" here means the utensils of the temple, such as cups, bowls, and containers used in worship. The word "brought forth" means he had carried them from one place to another.

The author of the book, whom tradition usually identifies with Ezra, recounts the return of the Jews after the exile. Cyrus allowed them to go back to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple, and the text says that God stirred up their spirit. Returning these objects was part of that permission.

For today: God can work even through people who do not know him, and what seemed lost can be restored. If you feel today that something valuable has been lost in your life, trust that God is still working with patience and can return it to its purpose.
exp.7:9:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned to Jerusalem. It names a leader from the family of Shelomith, the son of Josiphiah, who traveled with 160 males. The word "males" refers to adult men, probably heads of households. Some translations read "the sons of Bani, Shelomith," and scholars are not sure how the original name was written.

Ezra, a priest and scribe, is the one who tells the story in the first person. Around 458 B.C., he led a group of Jews from Babylon to Jerusalem with permission from King Artaxerxes. He recorded the names carefully to keep a record of who took part in this return and in the spiritual rebuilding of the people.

For today: God knows and values each person, even those who go unnoticed. Your simple service, like that of these men, counts before Him. Serve faithfully wherever you are, without needing recognition.
exp.4:9:
This verse says that the Persian officials also asked the Jewish leaders what their names were, so that they could report to the king and record in writing the names of the men who were leading the work. The phrase "chief of them" means "leaders" or "at the head." "With speed" is a way of saying "quickly."

The speaker is Tatnai, governor of the region west of the Euphrates River, together with his companions. They write a letter to King Darius because the Jews were rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem and they wanted to know whether the Jews had permission. The names would serve as an official record. Here they only report what they saw and asked, without accusing anyone.

For today: God works through people with names and faces, and sometimes others observe us and ask us for explanations. Live your service with honesty and openness, so that if someone asks why you do what you do, you can answer with clarity and confidence in God.
exp.6:26:
This verse is a song of praise to God. Ezra says "Blessed be the Lord God of our fathers," meaning he blesses God and acknowledges him, because God placed in the king's heart the desire to honor the temple in Jerusalem. The phrase "such a thing as this" refers to everything the king allowed and commanded for the temple and for Ezra.

The one speaking is Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law. He has just read the letter from King Artaxerxes, which gave him support, resources, and authority to return to Jerusalem. Ezra does not give the credit to the king or to his own effort, but to God, who works even in the heart of a foreign ruler.

For today: when you receive help or an open door you did not expect, stop and give thanks to God. He can move circumstances and people, and recognizing this keeps us humble and trusting.
exp.1:52:
This verse names three families: the children of Barkos, the children of Sisera, and the children of Thamah. They belong to those called servants of the temple, a group who served in the house of God. The phrase "children of" means descendants or members of that family.

Ezra presents the list of those who returned from exile in Babylon to Judah, under the leadership of Zerubbabel. The text is a record, not a speech. The names are written down so it would be known who belonged to the people and who could serve in the temple. About the origin of these particular families we know little, and it is not fitting to invent details.

For today: God notices people who seem unimportant. These families have almost no history, yet they were recorded. Your simple and steady service, even if no one applauds it, has value before God. Serve faithfully wherever you are.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that the neighbors of the Jews who were going to return to Jerusalem encouraged them and supported them by giving objects of silver and gold, goods, animals, and valuable things. All of this was in addition to the freewill offerings that the people had already given. The phrase "strengthened their hands" is an old expression meaning to strengthen, encourage, and help. "Goods" refers to property or possessions.

The account in Ezra tells of the return from exile in Babylon, after the decree of King Cyrus of Persia. The narrator says that God stirred the spirit of the leaders and of many others to rebuild the temple. Those who stayed in those lands, probably both Jews and neighbors, helped with resources for the journey and the work.

For today: when someone undertakes something good, they cannot always do it alone. We can encourage and help with whatever we have, whether money, time, advice, or prayer. Generous support strengthens others to finish what God has placed on their heart.
exp.7:2:
This verse is part of a list of families who returned to Jerusalem. It says that from the descendants of Shechaniah, from the family of Pharosh (another way of writing Paros), came Zechariah, and that with him were counted one hundred and fifty men. "Of the sons of Shechaniah" and "by genealogy of the males" refers to the men of the family being recorded in the register.

The one speaking is Ezra, the priest and scribe, who tells how he went up from Babylon to Jerusalem in the time of King Artaxerxes. He carefully records the names of the heads of families and how many accompanied them. This shows who made up the people and who returned to rebuild the life of the temple. Some details of the name Shechaniah in this text are debated by scholars.

God knows each person by name, even when they seem to be just part of a list. Today we can remember that our service, though simple and little seen, matters. Take part faithfully in your church and in your family.
exp.9:1:
Shechaniah acknowledges before Ezra that the people have been unfaithful, that is, they have broken faith with God by marrying foreign women from the neighboring peoples. But he does not stop at guilt: he says that there is still hope for Israel. Sincere repentance leaves the door open to a new beginning.

Shechaniah was of the family of Elam, and several members of his family were involved in this problem. He speaks after seeing Ezra weeping and praying. The law warned that such marriages could turn the people's hearts toward other gods. What follows in the text, the decision to send those women away, is difficult, and it has been much debated how it should be understood.

For today: when you fail, do not remain alone in shame. Acknowledge your mistake honestly, trust that God offers hope, and take the first concrete step to correct your course.
exp.1:31:
It says that 320 descendants of the family of Harim returned to Judah. "Children of" does not refer only to direct sons, but to descendants of a common ancestor or clan. It is one figure within a long list of families.

The author of the book, whom tradition identifies with Ezra, records who returned from exile in Babylon, in the time of Zerubbabel and Joshua. The Jews were going back to their land to rebuild the temple and the life of the people. Nehemiah 7:35 gives the same figure for this family. The list shows that God cared for his people and that every family counted.

Today, this reminds us that God does not see his people as a faceless mass. Even when your service seems small or little seen, he remembers it. Serve faithfully wherever you are.
exp.2:2:
They say the Israelites who returned from exile set the altar on its old foundations. Although they were afraid of the peoples living around them, they offered burnt offerings on it to the Lord, that is, animals burned completely as a total surrender to God. They did this every morning and every evening.

The text is narrative; no one is speaking. The storyteller presents the returned exiles in Jerusalem, under the priest Jeshua and the governor Zerubbabel. The temple had not yet been rebuilt, but they put the altar in place first and began to worship according to the law of Moses. The "peoples of the lands" were the inhabitants of the region, who probably viewed the newcomers with suspicion.

For today: do not wait until you are free of fear before you begin to worship and obey God. They had fear, but they put God first. Today you can set aside a fixed moment every morning and every evening to pray, even when your circumstances remain uncertain.
exp.5:5:
This verse is part of King Darius's letter to the Persian governors west of the Euphrates River. He tells Tatnai, Shethar-boznai, and their companions, who are officials of the empire, to stay away from Jerusalem, that is, to stop getting in the way of the work on the temple.

The Jews had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple. Tatnai and his men doubted that they had permission, so they wrote to the king. Darius ordered a search of the records and found the decree of Cyrus that authorized the work. So Darius, as the supreme authority, confirms the permission and orders that no one interfere.

For today: when God has a work underway, the obstacles are sometimes removed by unexpected means, even through authorities who do not know him. Stay faithful in what God has entrusted to you, and trust that he knows how to open doors in his own time.
exp.8:10:
Here Ezra recalls that God had already warned Israel through the prophets. They were told that the land they were about to enter was unclean, meaning morally defiled by the practices of the people who lived there. The word "filled" in the verse means completely full, and the phrase "from one end to another" means from end to end. The "abominations" are practices that God regarded as detestable.

Ezra prays to God on behalf of the people. Some Jews who had returned from exile had intermarried with the neighboring peoples, and this was pulling them away from God's commandments. Ezra confesses the sin with shame and acknowledges that God was merciful in allowing them to return and rebuild.

The prophets cited do not appear in these exact words in any single book, so this is best understood as a summary of several warnings.

Today we can ask ourselves what influences draw us away from God without our noticing. With humility, we can confess our failings to him and choose to surround ourselves with what brings us closer to him.
exp.9:19:
This verse is part of a list of names. It says that two descendants of Immer, Hanani and Zebadiah, were found among the priests who had married foreign women. Immer was a well-known priestly family.

The book of Ezra tells of the return of the Jews from exile. The author records in detail the names of those who acknowledged their wrongdoing. The main problem was that these marriages could draw the people away from God and from his covenant. Interpreters debate how to apply today that decision, so harsh as sending away the wives, and the text gives no further personal details about these two men.
