For today: God takes account of each person, even those who appear only as a name in a list. He also invites us to acknowledge our failings with sincerity and to correct our course, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.7:23:
Ezra tells us that he set apart twelve of the leading priests. Among them he names Sherebiah and Hashabiah, and he added ten of their brothers. The word "separated" means that he set them apart or chose them for a special task.

Ezra, the priest and teacher of the law, was leading a group of Jews back to Jerusalem from Babylon. He had told the king that God takes care of those who seek him, so he was ashamed to ask for soldiers. For that reason they fasted and prayed. Now Ezra entrusts the offerings of silver, gold, and the vessels for the temple to these men. It is commonly understood that the number twelve recalls the twelve tribes of Israel, although the text does not explain this.

For today: if we say that we trust God, we should also act with order, openness, and responsibility. Faith and good stewardship go together, especially when we handle resources that belong to others.
exp.1:57:
This verse is a summary of the count of two groups who returned from exile in Babylon: the Nethinims and the descendants of Solomon's servants. Together they numbered 392 people. The Nethinims were helpers of the temple, dedicated to service tasks. The term for them, in the sense of those given over or set apart for that work, is what the verse names directly.

Ezra is the one who writes this list of the families who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. The purpose was to keep a record of who belonged to the people and what service was assigned to them. In this way the life of the rebuilt temple was put in order. Even groups with different origins were recorded.

For today: God takes notice of humble and hidden service. Perhaps no one applauds what you do in your church or in your home, but God does not forget your name or your effort. Serve with faithfulness and joy.
exp.6:18:
This verse says that Ezra is to take to Jerusalem the vessels that were given to him for the service of the temple. The word "restore" means to give back or put back in its proper place. Those objects were for worship, and they were to be presented before God, that is, for use in worship.

The speaker is King Artaxerxes, in an official letter addressed to Ezra, a priest and scribe of the law. The king gives him permission, silver, gold and equipment so that worship in Jerusalem can be re-established. The temple vessels had been carried away years before, and now they are returning. This shows how God moved a king to favor his people.

For today: what God entrusts to us, such as gifts, time or resources, we should care for and use faithfully in his service, not for ourselves.
exp.2:8:
This verse names the Levites who joined together to oversee the rebuilding of the temple. Jeshua, Kadmiel and the sons of Henadad, together with their families, "as one man," that is, united, were in charge of pressing forward and urging on those who were doing the work. The name "Judah" here seems to refer to another Levite named Hodaviah, though some understand it differently.

This is a narrative passage, probably written by Ezra. It tells what happened when the Jews returned from exile in Babylon, around the second year after their return, and began laying the foundations of the temple in Jerusalem, with the permission of King Cyrus.

Today, good work moves forward when people come together and each one takes on their part. In the church, the family or the workplace, serving with a shared purpose and encouraging one another makes possible what we could not accomplish alone.
exp.3:23:
This verse says that the building of the temple in Jerusalem came to a halt. It stayed stopped until the second year of the reign of Darius, king of Persia. The word that is quoted here means that the work was stopped or brought to a standstill.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Ezra, who recounts what happened. The enemies of the Jews had written to King Artaxerxes, and he ordered the work to be stopped. Then Rehum and Shimshai went to Jerusalem and halted the work by force. This verse serves as a bridge: the temple work remained stopped for years, until the time of Darius. Some scholars debate how exactly the kings mentioned in this part of the account fit together.

For today: sometimes the projects we undertake for God are stalled by opposition or by circumstances. A pause does not mean that God has changed his mind. We can wait with patience, keep praying, and be ready to resume the task when the door opens.
exp.9:9:
Ezra the priest stands up before the people and tells them plainly that they have failed. "Transgressed" means betraying or breaking a serious commitment to God. "Strange wives" refers to foreign women, and Ezra says that by marrying them, they added more guilt to the guilt Israel already carried.

Ezra, a priest and teacher of the law, speaks after the return from exile in Babylon. The people are gathered in Jerusalem, trembling because of the seriousness of the matter and because of the rain. The main concern was that these marriages would lead them to follow other gods, as had happened before in Israel's history. There are different views on how to apply this passage today.

For today: God invites us to acknowledge our failures without excuses. When someone speaks to us with truth and love, we can respond with humility, return to God, and correct our course.
exp.9:43:
This verse closes the list of men who had married foreign women.

It is the end of the book of Ezra. The author, whom tradition usually identifies with Ezra, records the names of those who had broken God's law by marrying women from neighboring peoples, because of the risk that Israel would turn away from God. He says that some of them had children, and the Bible does not explain in detail what happened to them. There are different views on how to understand that decision, which was so hard.

Today we can learn that faithfulness to God sometimes requires difficult decisions. It is worth examining our relationships and habits, and asking God for wisdom, humility, and compassion so that we may act with truth and with love.
exp.5:14:
This verse says that the temple in Jerusalem was finished on the third day of the month Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of Darius. "Was finished" means that the work was brought to completion. Adar is the last month of the Jewish calendar, falling between February and March. It is generally understood to correspond to the year 516 BC, although exact dates are calculated in different ways.

The author of the book tells the story of the return of the Jews from exile. The work had been halted by opposition, and was then resumed with the encouragement of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah. The text emphasizes that the temple was completed by God's command and with the support of the Persian kings.

For today: God knows how to bring to completion what He begins, even when there are delays and obstacles. Keep faithfully doing what He has entrusted to you, and do not lose heart.
exp.3:11:
This verse is part of a letter of accusation. It says that some Jews, who had come from the king's territory and arrived in Jerusalem, were rebuilding the city. They call it "the rebellious and the bad city." The word "notorious" would mean well known or obvious, and "set up the walls" means they were already repairing the foundations.

The writers are officials and neighbors in the region, in the time of the Persian king Artaxerxes. The Jews who had returned from exile were rebuilding Jerusalem, and these opponents wanted to stop them. They present their complaint as loyalty to the king, but what they were really after was halting the work. Then they appeal to the king's treasury and honor to convince him.

For today: not everything that sounds like concern for the common good is sincere. When someone accuses you or opposes the good you are doing, stay calm, examine your heart, and trust God, who knows the truth.
exp.1:43:
The verse continues a list of families of the Nethinim, a word that means "given" or "dedicated." They were temple servants who helped the Levites with the humblest tasks. Three families are named here: Keros, Siaha, and Padon, who returned to Jerusalem.

Tradition attributes the book to Ezra, who records who came back from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. The list showed who belonged to the people and to their service in the temple. The exact origin of the temple servants is not certain. Some think they descended from the Gibeonites, but this cannot be affirmed with certainty.

For today: God remembers the names of those who serve without being seen. Serve faithfully in small things, even when no one applauds you; God sees it and values it.
exp.1:23:
This verse says that 42 people from Azmaveth returned from exile. "Children of" here means descendants or inhabitants of that place. Azmaveth seems to have been a town near Anathoth, in the territory of Benjamin, though some scholars doubt the exact details.

The book of Ezra keeps this list of the Jews who came back from Babylon to Judah, after decades of exile. The one who wrote it, traditionally Ezra, wanted to record who answered the call to rebuild the temple and the life of the people. The names and numbers show that this history was real and that each group was counted.

For today: God does not overlook anyone, even when their group is small. Your faithfulness in ordinary things, such as serving in your church or helping your family, is also noted before Him and has value.
exp.3:5:
This verse says that at the beginning of Ahasuerus's reign, the enemies of the Jews wrote accusations against the people of Judah and Jerusalem. The king is identified as the Persian ruler who in Hebrew is called Jashvérosh, usually identified with Xerxes I.

The book of Ezra recounts the opposition faced by the Jews who returned from exile to rebuild the temple and the city. The author of the book is the narrator, and here he summarizes several attacks that came from neighboring peoples across different kings. Some scholars think the author groups these episodes by theme rather than in chronological order, which is why kings who came after Darius appear here.

For today: when you do good and someone accuses you or discourages you, do not be surprised. Keep going with patience, act with integrity, and trust that God sees what others do not see.
exp.4:8:
This verse is part of a letter that some Persian officials wrote to King Darius. They report that they questioned the elders of the Jews, asking: "Who commanded you to build this house, and to make up these walls?"

The speakers are Tatnai, the governor of the region west of the Euphrates River, and his companions. When they saw that the work on the temple was moving along quickly, they wanted to know whether it had official backing. So they wrote to the king so that he could confirm it. The Jews would answer that they serve the God of heaven and earth.

Today, when someone questions something you are doing with good intentions, answer calmly, clearly, and truthfully. If we serve God, we can explain our faith with respect, without fear, and without becoming defensive.

sum.8: The leaders report to Ezra that the people, including priests and officials, have married women from the neighboring nations and have taken up their practices. Ezra tears his clothes, is overcome with grief, and prays in shame, acknowledging the people's guilt, thanking God for his mercy, and admitting that they do not deserve to stand in his presence.
sum.4: The prophets Haggai and Zechariah encouraged the people, and Zerubbabel and Joshua began to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. Tattenai, the governor of the region, asked them who had given them permission and wrote to King Darius. The elders explained that Cyrus had given the order, and the text says that God was watching over them.
sum.3: The enemies of Judah offered to help rebuild the temple, but Zerubbabel and the leaders refused the offer, because King Cyrus had assigned that work to them alone. The adversaries then discouraged them and brought accusations against them before King Artaxerxes, who ordered the work to stop. Construction was halted until the second year of Darius.
sum.1: This chapter lists the Israelites who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah with Zerubbabel and other leaders: families, priests, Levites, singers, and temple servants. Some priests were set aside because their record of descent could not be found. On arrival, several heads of families gave freewill offerings to rebuild the house of God, and everyone settled in their own towns.
sum.5: King Darius had the royal archives searched, and they found the decree of Cyrus, which authorized rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem with the king's support. Darius ordered the neighboring governors not to interfere, and to help cover the costs. The temple was finished and dedicated with joy, and they celebrated the Passover, because God had given them happiness.
sum.2: The Israelites who had returned from exile gathered in Jerusalem, rebuilt the altar, and began offering sacrifices to God again, even though they were afraid of their neighbors. Then they started laying the foundations of the temple amid songs of praise. The people celebrated with joy, while the elders, who remembered the former temple, wept.
sum.9: Ezra prays and weeps, and the people join him in repentance for having married foreign women. They promise to make a covenant with God and to send these wives away, and an investigation is organized in every town. At the end, the chapter lists the priests, Levites, and other men who had committed this sin.
sum.6: Ezra, a priest and scribe who knew the law of Moses well, went up from Babylon to Jerusalem with a group of Israelites, because God was with him. King Artaxerxes gave him a letter with silver, gold, supplies, and authority to teach and to judge. Ezra praised God for having moved the king's heart.
sum.0: In the first year of Cyrus, king of Persia, God moved his heart to let the Jews return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple, fulfilling what Jeremiah had said. Many were moved to return, their neighbors helped them with offerings, and Cyrus gave back the temple vessels. In this way we see that God keeps his word.
sum.7: Ezra gathers the families who are returning from Babylon and, noticing that there are no Levites among them, arranges for ministers to serve in the temple. Before the journey he fasts with the people and trusts in God's protection instead of asking the king for soldiers. God watches over them on the road, they faithfully deliver the offerings in Jerusalem, and they worship God.
